lakshana_iast: prajñāpūrvakavyāpāravattvaṃ jīvatvam |
meaning_short: Possessing purposeful activity preceded by conscious intelligence is the defining essence of the sentient soul (Jīva).
meaning_deep: Unlike insentient matter (jaḍa), whose motion is mechanical, a sentient being acts through cognition, desire, and volitional effort (jñāna-icchā-prayatna). In Tattvavāda, every Jīva is eternally distinct from Paramātman and from all other Jīvas, atomic in measure, self-luminous as 'I' to its own Sākṣī, and exercises real yet God-dependent agency (parādhīna-kartṛtva). In supreme mahāyoga, Madhvācārya also derives 'Jīva' for Viṣṇu Himself ('viṣṇur jīva iti proktaḥ satataṃ prāṇadhāraṇāt' — VTN 1.81) as the constant sustainer of vital breath.

meaning_short: That which is apprehended in primary, immediate cognition as 'it is' (asti) is a Bhāva (positive entity).
meaning_deep: Rather than circularly defining positive being as the negation of non-being, Jayatīrtha grounds Bhāva phenomenologically in first-order cognition: when awareness encounters an entity and directly registers 'it exists' without prior reference to a counterpositive (pratiyogin), that entity is Bhāva — comprising both Cetana (sentient) and Acetana (insentient) reals.

meaning_short: That which is cognized in initial apprehension as 'it is not' (nāsti) is Abhāva (real absence), which is threefold: prior, posterior, and eternal.
meaning_deep: Against schools that dismiss absence as a mere figure of speech for the bare floor, Madhvācārya and Jayatīrtha defend Abhāva as an objective dependent category apprehended as 'there is no pot here'. lakshana_iast: mahattattvopādānakam ahaṅkāratattvam | vaikārikataijasatāmasabhedena trividham |
meaning_short: Ahaṅkāra-tattva is the cosmic Principle of Individuation evolved from Mahat, divided threefold into Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa.
meaning_deep: From Vaikārika (sāttvika) Ahaṅkāra arises the cosmic Manas; from Taijasa (rājasa) arise the ten Indriyas; and from Tāmasa arise the five subtle Tanmātras and through them the five gross elements. Garuḍa, Śeṣa, and Rudra are its chief presiding deities.

english_glosses: mind; internal organ of thought
phonetic_aliases: manas; manah; antahkarana; mind
lakshana_deva: वैकारिकाहङ्कारोपादानकं मनस्तत्त्वम् । तत्त्वभिन्नं मन इन्द्रियं नित्यमनित्यं चेति द्विविधम् ।
lakshana_iast: vaikārikāhaṅkāropādānakaṃ manastattvam | tattvabhinnaṃ mana indriyaṃ nityam anityaṃ ceti dvividham |
meaning_short: Manas (Mind) is both the cosmic principle evolved from Vaikārika Ahaṅkāra and the internal cognitive organ — eternal as Svarūpa-manas, transient as the fivefold prākṛta mind.
meaning_deep: In transmigrating beings, the external prākṛta internal organ functions in five modes — manas (deliberation), buddhi (decision), ahaṅkāra (egoity), citta (recollection), and cetanā — and serves as the instrument of memory (smṛti) and meditation (dhyāna).

english_glosses: sense faculty; cognitive or motor organ
phonetic_aliases: indriya; indriyam; jnanendriya; karmendriya; senses
lakshana_deva: प्रमातृस्वरूपं प्राकृतं चेति द्विविधमिन्द्रियम् । ज्ञानेन्द्रियाणि पञ्च कर्मेन्द्रियाणि पञ्च मनश्चेति ।
lakshana_iast: pramātṛsvarūpaṃ prākṛtaṃ ceti dvividham indriyam | jñānendriyāṇi pañca karmendriyāṇi pañca manaś ceti |
meaning_short: Indriya (faculty) is twofold: the eternal intrinsic Sākṣī-faculty identical with the knower's essence, and the material tenfold cognitive/motor organs evolved from Taijasa Ahaṅkāra.
meaning_deep: By distinguishing Svarūpendriya (Sākṣī) from Prākṛtendriya, Jayatīrtha explains how liberated souls perceive bliss and cosmos without material bodies, and how embodied souls directly intuit self, time, mind, bliss, and pain even when outer senses are shut.

english_glosses: subtle element; proto-sensory essence
phonetic_aliases: tanmatra; tanmaatra; pancatanmatra; subtle elements
lakshana_deva: मीयन्त इति मात्राः शब्दस्पर्शरूपरसगन्धाः । तामसाहङ्कारजन्याः पञ्चतन्मात्रा इत्युच्यन्ते ।
lakshana_iast: mīyanta iti mātrāḥ śabdasparśarūparasagandhāḥ | tāmasāhaṅkārajanyāḥ pañcatanmātrā ity ucyante |
meaning_short: Because objects are measured/cognized through them, sound, touch, form, taste, and scent are 'mātrās'; their subtle substantial essences born of Tāmasa Ahaṅkāra are the five Tanmātras.
meaning_deep: Dvaita carefully separates Tanmātras as cosmic subtle substances (tattva-rūpāḥ dravyāṇi) that serve as material causes of the five gross elements from ordinary sensible qualities (tattva-bhinnāḥ guṇāḥ) residing in objects.

english_glosses: five great elements; ether, air, fire, water, earth
phonetic_aliases: pancabhuta; panchabhuta; bhuta; mahabhuta; elements
lakshana_deva: तन्मात्राद्वारा तामसाहङ्कारजन्यानि पञ्चभूतानि आकाशवायुतेजोऽप्पृथिव्यः ।
lakshana_iast: tanmātrādvārā tāmasāhaṅkārajanyāni pañcabhūtāni ākāśavāyutejo'ppṛthivyaḥ |
meaning_short: The five great elements — ether, air, fire, water, and earth — evolved from Tāmasa Ahaṅkāra through the mediation of the five Tanmātras.
meaning_deep: Following the Bhāgavata principle of cumulative qualities (uttara-uttara-guṇānuvṛtti), ether bears sound; air bears sound and touch; fire adds form; water adds taste; and earth possesses all five qualities.

english_glosses: spiritual ignorance; beginningless bondage-veil
phonetic_aliases: avidya; avidyaa; ajnana; jivaacchadika; paramaacchadika
lakshana_deva: जीवाच्छादिका परमाच्छादिका चेति सकारात्मकं द्रव्यमविद्या । सर्वाऽप्यविद्या जीवाश्रिता प्रातिस्विकी च ।
lakshana_iast: jīvācchādikā paramācchādikā ceti sakārātmakaṃ dravyam avidyā | sarvā'py avidyā jīvāśritā prātisvikī ca |
meaning_short: Avidyā (spiritual ignorance) is a real, positive subtle substance resting uniquely on each bound Jīva, veiling both the Jīva's own innate bliss (jīvācchādikā) and the Supreme Lord (paramācchādikā).
meaning_deep: In radical contrast to Advaita's single cosmic anirvacanīya Avidyā resting on Brahman, Madhvācārya holds that Avidyā is genuinely real (satya), strictly individual to each Jīva (prātisvikī), never touches Brahman, is sustained by the Lord's Māyā-will, and is destroyed only by His grace upon Aparokṣa-jñāna.

english_glosses: phoneme; eternal letter-sound; syllable
phonetic_aliases: varna; varnah; akshara; alphabet; phoneme
lakshana_deva: वर्णा अकारादय एकपञ्चाशत् प्रत्येकं व्याप्ता अनादिनित्याश्च । उच्चारणध्वनिव्यङ्ग्याः ।
lakshana_iast: varṇā akārādaya ekapañcāśat pratyekaṃ vyāptā anādinityāś ca | uccāraṇadhvanivyaṅgyāḥ |
meaning_short: The fifty-one Sanskrit phonemes (Varṇas) beginning with 'a' are each all-pervasive, beginninglessly eternal substances, manifested — not created — by vocalized sound (dhvani).
meaning_deep: Dvaita rejects both the Nyāya view that letters are transient qualities of ether (śabda-anitya-vāda) and the Vaiyākaraṇa sphoṭa entity over and above letters. Every phoneme is kūṭastha-nitya; this eternal ontology of Varṇas grounds both the unauthored eternity of the Veda and the sacred Mātṛkā-vidyā.

english_glosses: darkness; positive obscuring substance
phonetic_aliases: andhakara; tamah; darkness
lakshana_deva: प्रकाशनिवार्योऽन्धकारः । न तु तेजोऽभावः स्वातन्त्र्येणोपलभ्यमानत्वात् ।
lakshana_iast: prakāśanivāryo'ndhakāraḥ | na tu tejo'bhāvaḥ svātantryeṇopalabhyamānatvāt |
meaning_short: Darkness (Andhakāra) is a positive substance dispelled by light — not the mere absence of light, because it is perceived positively in its own right.
meaning_deep: Against Nyāya's claim that darkness is merely tejo'bhāva (absence of light), Dvaita proves Andhakāra is a distinct blue-black positive substance (dravya) because perceiving an absence requires prior remembrance of the counterpositive, whereas darkness is directly perceived as concealing things and bearing colour.

english_glosses: latent impression; subliminal trace
phonetic_aliases: vasana; vaasana; samskara; svapna; dream
lakshana_deva: स्वाप्नपदार्थोपादानानि वासनाः । पूर्वानुभवजन्या मनोगताः प्रवाहतोऽनादयः ।
lakshana_iast: svāpnapadārthopādānāni vāsanāḥ | pūrvānubhavajanyā manogatāḥ pravāhato'nādayaḥ |
meaning_short: Vāsanās (latent mental impressions) are subtle substances lodged in the mind, born of prior experiences, serving as the real material cause of dream objects.
meaning_deep: In Madhvācārya's realist dream theory, dreams are not illusory non-entities: the indwelling Lord creates genuine, transient dream-chariots and dream-worlds out of the beginningless stream of subtle vāsanā-matter stored in the Jīva's mind (`vāsanāmātram` — BSB 3.2.3). What is false in a dream is only the dreamer's mistaking the internal vāsanā-object for an external waking object.

phonetic_aliases: kala; kaala; time; kalah; pravaha
lakshana_deva: आयुर्व्यवस्थापकः कालः । प्रकृत्योत्पत्तिविनाशवान् कालप्रवाहस्तु नित्यः ।
lakshana_iast: āyurvyavasthāpakaḥ kālaḥ | prakṛtyotpattivināśavān kālapravāhas tu nityaḥ |
meaning_short: Time (Kāla) is the regulator of lifespans and universal succession; its individual moments arise and perish from subtle Prakṛti, while its stream (pravāha) is eternal.
meaning_deep: How do we know Time even in deep sleep ('sukham aham asvāpsam — I slept happily for so long')? Madhvācārya answers: Time is intuited directly by the Sākṣī, and its unbroken stream of moments (kṣaṇa, lava) ensures there is never a timeless void before creation or during pralaya.

meaning_short: Joy or Bliss (Sukha) is that which is intrinsically experienced as congenial and favourable to oneself.
meaning_deep: Dvaita divides Sukha into (1) eternal Svarūpa-sukha — infinite and independent in Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, finite and graded in Muktiyogya Jīvas, manifest in Mokṣa — and (2) transient mental sukha experienced in worldly life.

lakshana_iast: pratikūlatayā vedanīyaṃ duḥkham |
meaning_short: Sorrow or Suffering (Duḥkha) is that which is directly experienced as adverse and repugnant to oneself.
meaning_deep: Paramātman and Mahālakṣmī are eternally untouched by Duḥkha (aduḥkhaspṛṣṭa). For Muktiyogyas, sorrow is strictly extrinsic and ends forever at Mokṣa; only in Tamoyogyas does sorrow belong to latent dark svarūpa.

lakshana_iast: kāma icchā | sā nityānityabhedād duṣṭāduṣṭabhedena ca dvividhā |
meaning_short: Volitional desire or will (Icchā) is cognitive conation toward an object, divided into eternal and transient, and into pure (aduṣṭa) and tainted (duṣṭa).
meaning_deep: The Lord's eternal, unfrustrated Will (satya-saṅkalpa) is wholly pure and effortless; in bound souls, mental desire mediates between cognition (jñāna) and effort (prayatna).

lakshana_deva: प्रवृत्तिः प्रयत्नः । नित्यानित्यभेदात् सोऽपि द्विविधः ।
lakshana_iast: pravṛttiḥ prayatnaḥ | nityānityabhedāt so'pi dvividhaḥ |
meaning_short: Volitional effort (Prayatna) is active conative exertion (pravṛtti), which is eternal in essence for sentient beings and transient in mental modifications.
meaning_deep: Prayatna completes the triad `jñāna → icchā → prayatna` that constitutes `prajñāpūrvaka-vyāpāra`, the hallmark of Jīvatva. Even the Jīva's real Prayatna operates under the sustaining permission and power of Paramātman (`parāttu tacchruteḥ` — BSB 2.3.41).

phonetic_aliases: dharma; punya; punyam; sukrita; righteousness; merit

lakshana_iast: vihitakarmajanyo bhagavatprītihetuḥ puṇyākhyo guṇo dharmaḥ |
meaning_short: Dharma (Puṇya) is spiritual merit generated by scripturally enjoined acts that pleases Bhagavān; when desireless (akāmya), it purifies the mind for direct realization.
meaning_deep: Remarkably, Dvaita holds that righteous worship and service performed even after Aparokṣa-jñāna is not futile: it manifests intrinsic merit (nitya-puṇya) that enhances the lustre of bliss in Mokṣa (`ānandātiśaya-hetuḥ`).

english_glosses: fructifying karma; operative past action
phonetic_aliases: prarabdha; praarabdha; prarabdham; sancita; karmakshaya
lakshana_deva: भोक्तुमारब्धं प्रारब्धम् । सञ्चितं भोक्तव्यमप्रारब्धम् । प्रारब्धपुण्यपापयोस्तु भोगेनैव विनाशः ।
lakshana_iast: bhoktum ārabdhaṃ prārabdham | sañcitaṃ bhoktavyam aprārabdham | prārabdhapuṇyapāpayos tu bhogenaiva vināśaḥ |
meaning_short: Prārabdha is that portion of past karma which has already begun yielding embodied experience; unlike uncommenced (sañcita) karma burnt by realization, prārabdha is exhausted through experience (or graciously pared down by the Lord).
meaning_deep: Upon Aparokṣa-jñāna, all accumulated uncommenced sin and undesired merit are destroyed, but commenced karma (prārabdha) continues across remaining ordained lifetimes until the soul bathes in the Virajā river and sheds its subtle body.

meaning_short: Innate Aptitude (Haṭha / Svarūpa-yogyatā) is the beginningless intrinsic nature of each soul that grounds its spiritual path, capacity for devotion, and graded destiny.
meaning_deep: Why do souls respond differently to identical teachings under an impartial Lord? Madhvācārya locates the ultimate differentiator in each Jīva's beginningless intrinsic disposition (anādi-svarūpa-yogyatā), freeing God of arbitrariness (vaiṣamya) and cruelty (nairghṛṇya).

meaning_short: Śama (inner serenity) is the unwavering, one-pointed resting of the intellect in Bhagavān.
meaning_deep: One of Śrī Madhvācārya's most celebrated definitions! Whereas other schools define Śama negatively as mere mental blankness or suppression of thoughts, Madhvācārya defines it positively and theocentrically: true quietude of intellect is its steadfast absorption in Viṣṇu (`śamo manoniṣṭhatā paramātmani`).

lakshana_iast: sukhaduḥkhādidvandvasahiṣṇutā titikṣā |
meaning_short: Titikṣā (forbearance) is unruffled endurance of dualities such as pleasure and pain, heat and cold, honour and dishonour.
meaning_deep: In Tattvavāda sādhana, Titikṣā arises from knowing that all pleasant and painful fruits arrive under the wise governance of the Supreme Lord according to one's prārabdha, freeing the seeker from lamentation and resentment.

lakshana_iast: parāpekṣāṃ vinā kāryānukūlaguṇo balam |
meaning_short: Strength (Bala) is the intrinsic quality conducive to accomplishing effects without exhaustion or reliance on extraneous props.
meaning_deep: In its plenary, absolute sense (`parāpekṣāṃ vinā`), Bala belongs supremely to Bhagavān (`pūrṇāvyayātmabalacitsukhavīryasāraḥ` — MBTN 1.13) and secondarily, by His gift, to Mukhyaprāṇa Vāyu and all sentient souls according to tāratamya.

english_glosses: creation; cosmic manifestation
phonetic_aliases: srishti; srushti; janma; creation; ashtakartritva
lakshana_deva: जन्माद्यस्य यतः । विशेषाप्तिर्विकारः स्याज्जननं नाम वस्तुनः ।
lakshana_iast: janmādy asya yataḥ | viśeṣāptir vikāraḥ syāj jananaṃ nāma vastunaḥ |
meaning_short: Creation (Sṛṣṭi) is the Lord's imparting of new manifest states (viśeṣāpti / parādhīna-viśeṣāpti) to eternal substrates and evolving cosmos from Prakṛti.
meaning_deep: In Brahmasūtra 1.1.2 (`janmādy asya yataḥ`), Madhvācārya shows that Brahman is defined as the sole independent cause of the eightfold cosmic functions (aṣṭakartṛtva): sṛṣṭi, sthiti, saṃhāra, niyamana, jñāna, ajñāna, bandha, and mokṣa. Even eternal entities undergo 'parādhīna-viśeṣāpti' — acquisition of new relational states dependent on the Lord.

meaning_short: The Waking State (Jāgrat) is outward-turned cognition perceiving external objects through outer senses, governed by Bhagavān in His Viśva form seated in the right eye.
meaning_deep: In Māṇḍūkya Bhāṣya, Madhvācārya clarifies that 'Viśva', 'Taijasa', 'Prājña', and 'Turīya' are primarily four cosmic-indwelling forms of Bhagavān Viṣṇu Himself who orchestrate the Jīva's waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and liberated states.

english_glosses: dream state; inward subtle experience

lakshana_iast: jāgraddarśanasaṃskārarūpatvāt svapnagaṃ tu yat | antaḥprajñas tu taijasaḥ |
meaning_short: Dream (Svapna) is inward perception of real subtle forms shaped by Bhagavān Taijasa (seated in the throat/mind) out of latent waking impressions (vāsanās).
meaning_deep: Dream objects are real mental creations fashioned instantaneously by the Lord (`sandhye sṛṣṭir āha hi` — BS 3.2.1) from mental vāsanās to yield subtle karmic retribution or prophetic indications; only identifying them with gross external things is an error.

lakshana_iast: ghanaprajñas tathā prājñaḥ | uparatendriyamanovṛtter jīvasya hṛdaye prājñāliṅgitasya svarūpasukhānubhavaḥ suṣuptiḥ |
meaning_short: Deep Sleep (Suṣupti) is the state where outer senses and mind subside and the Jīva, embraced by Bhagavān Prājña in the heart-lotus, intuits its bare self, time, and a glimpse of innate ease via Sākṣī.
meaning_deep: Even when all material instruments rest in Suṣupti, the Jīva does not merge into undifferentiated identity with Brahman; held closely by Prājña Hari in the hṛdaya-ākāśa, its Sākṣī continues to witness innate sukha and kāla, enabling the waking memory 'I slept peacefully.'

english_glosses: the Fourth; transcendent liberating Lord

lakshana_iast: nivṛtteḥ sarvaduḥkhānām īśānaḥ prabhur avyayaḥ | sarvaduḥkhānāṃ nivṛtteḥ kāraṇabhūtas turīyo devo mokṣadaḥ samprakīrtitaḥ |
meaning_short: Turīya is the fourth transcendent form of Bhagavān Hari who completely terminates all sorrow and bestows eternal liberation (Mokṣa).
meaning_deep: In Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1.10 (`nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiḥprajñam...`), Advaita reads Turīya as an attribute-less Ātman; Madhvācārya demonstrates from the verse's own epithets (`īśānaḥ prabhur avyayaḥ`) that Turīya is the supreme personal Lord Viṣṇu, sovereign remover of all bondage.

english_glosses: devotion; supreme love of God

lakshana_deva: माहात्म्यज्ञानपूर्वस्तु सुदृढः सर्वतोऽधिकः । स्नेहो भक्तिरिति प्रोक्तस्तया मुक्तिर्न चान्यथा ॥
lakshana_iast: māhātmyajñānapūrvas tu sudṛḍhaḥ sarvato'dhikaḥ | sneho bhaktir iti proktas tayā muktir na cānyathā ||
meaning_short: Bhakti is unshakeable love for Bhagavān, preceded by true knowledge of His supreme majesty (māhātmya-jñāna) and surpassing love for all else — through it alone is liberation attained.
meaning_deep: Perhaps the single greatest verse in Tattvavāda soteriology (MBTN 1.85). Madhvācārya fuses knowledge and love into an indivisible whole: affection without knowledge of God's supremacy is mere sentiment, and dry knowledge without supreme love cannot win grace. Bhakti is simultaneously the means (sādhana) and continues in Mokṣa as parama-bhakti, an eternal outpouring of blissful love.

meaning_short: Vairāgya (dispassion) is detachment from craving selfish enjoyments both here and in celestial realms, awakened through discerning the threefold sorrow of saṃsāra and keeping company with the wise.
meaning_deep: In Dvaita, Vairāgya is not hatred of the real world created by Viṣṇu, but relinquishment of egoistic possessiveness (mamakāra) and sensual craving so that all things are seen as belonging to Hari and engaged in His service.

meaning_short: Śaraṇāgati (wholehearted refuge) is seeking sole shelter in the all-independent Lord Hari and dedicating all actions and fruits to Him in vivid awareness of one's utter dependence.

lakshana_iast: sadgurūpadeśena sacchāstrārthajñānarūpaṃ śravaṇam | ajñānanivartakam |
meaning_short: Śravaṇa is receptive study of the true import of sacred scripture through the instruction of a qualified Guru, dispelling initial ignorance (ajñāna).
meaning_deep: In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka triad `śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ`, Śravaṇa removes simple lack of knowledge (ajñāna), Manana removes doubt and contrary error (saṃśaya-viparyaya), and Nididhyāsana culminates in direct vision (aparokṣa).

phonetic_aliases: manana; mananam; mimamsa; vicara; jijnasa; reflection
lakshana_deva: श्रुतस्य तत्त्वस्य हृदीकरणाय मीमांसापरपर्यायो विचारो मननम् । संशयमिथ्याज्ञाननिरासकम् ।

lakshana_iast: sarpati vakragatinā gacchati iti sarpaḥ | sarpaḥ pṛdākur bhujago bhujaṅgo 'hir bhujaṅgamaḥ ||
meaning_short: A serpent or snake — a limbless reptile that glides sinuously upon its chest and perceives vibrations through its eyes.
meaning_deep: Derived directly from √sṛpḷ ('gatau' — `sarpati`, to glide sinuously, cognate with Latin *serpēns* and English *serpent*), `sarpa` fills Amarakośa's Bhogivarga (1.8.4–7) with anatomically vivid names: `ahi`, `bhujaṅga` / `bhujaga` ('moving in curves'), `uraga` ('gliding on its breast', `urasā gacchati`), `pannaga` ('not walking on feet', `padbhyāṃ na gacchati`), `phaṇin` ('hooded'), `pavanasana` ('feeding on air'), and `cakṣuḥśravas` ('hearing vibrations through its unblinking eyes'). meaning_deep: Yāska (Nirukta 6.27) and Uṇādi-sūtra (4.2: `madeḥ syaḥ`) derive `matsya` from √madī ('harṣe' — sporting joyfully in deep waters, `madanti apsu`). Devotional poets invoke `jala-matsya-nyāya` — just as a fish cannot live an instant parted from water, supreme `bhakti` cannot bear forgetfulness of Bhagavān, who Himself assumed the primordial `Matsya-avatāra` to rescue the Vedas.

meaning_short: A monkey or forest primate — the agile, branch-leaping woodland creature almost human in form and dexterity.
meaning_deep: Classical Sanskrit commentators offer two complementary derivations for `vānara`: (1) from `vana` ('belonging to the forest and thriving on woodland fruits', `vane bhavaḥ`) and (2) `vā naraḥ` ('almost like a man!', reflecting keen observation of primate intelligence and hands). meaning_short: An ant — the minute, tireless social insect celebrated in Sanskrit proverbs for disciplined perseverance.
meaning_deep: Formed by reduplication from √pīl ('moving in orderly files and gathering grain by grain'), `pipīlikā` (`pipīla` m.) represents the humblest scale of embodied consciousness (`ā-brahma-pipīlikā-paryantam` — 'from four-faced Brahmā down to the tiniest ant', a standard Vedāntic phrase affirming that Paramātman indwells every sentient soul without exception). meaning_short: A gentle smile — the serene, silent blossoming of the cheeks and eyes without baring the teeth or breaking into loud laughter.
meaning_deep: Derived from √ṣmiṅ ('īṣaddhasane' — to smile softly, cognate with English *smile*) with `-kta` expressing action (`bhāve ktaḥ`, Pāṇini 3.3.114), `smita` stands as the most refined of the six gradations of laughter in Bharata's *Nāṭyaśāstra* (6.52–55) and Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.35: `smita`, `hasita`, `vihasita`, `upahasita`, `apahasita`, `atihasita`). meaning_short: A voice, vowel, Vedic pitch accent, or musical note — pure self-resonant tone that shines forth of its own accord and delights the ear.
meaning_deep: Derived from √svṛ ('śabdopatāpayoḥ' — to sound, resonate), Patañjali's *Mahābhāṣya* (on Pāṇini 1.2.29) gives the classic grammatical nirukti: `svayaṃ rājante iti svarāḥ` — vowels (`ac`) shine independently without needing consonant crutches, just as `svara` in Vedic recitation denotes the three sacred pitch accents (`udātta`, `anudātta`, `svarita`). english_glosses: knowledge; cognition; awareness; spiritual realization
phonetic_aliases: jnana; gyana; bodha; samvid; avabodha; vijnana; knowledge
lakshana_deva: ज्ञायतेऽवगम्यतेऽर्थोऽनेन इति ज्ञानम् । सर्वव्यवहारहेतुर्गुणो बुद्धिर्ज्ञानम् ॥
lakshana_iast: jñāyate 'vagamyate 'rtho 'nena iti jñānam | sarvavyavahārahetur guṇo buddhir jñānam ||
meaning_short: Knowledge or awareness — the illuminating cognition whereby objects and reality become manifest to a knower.

lakshana_iast: gandhayate sūcayati svāśrayam iti gandhaḥ | ghrāṇagrāhyo guṇo gandhaḥ sa ca dvividhaḥ surabhir asurabhiś ca ||
meaning_short: Fragrance or scent — the olfactory quality inherent exclusively in the earth element (`pṛthivī`) and apprehended by the nose.
meaning_deep: Derived from √gandh ('sūcane' — delicately intimating its unseen floral or earthy source across the breeze), `gandha` is catalogued in Amarakośa (Guṇavarga 1.5.13) with `āmoda` ('far-wafting perfume'), `parimala`, and `saurabha` (sandalwood paste and lotus scent). In Tarkasaṅgraha (26: `ghrāṇagrāhyo guṇo gandhaḥ; pṛthivīmātravṛttiḥ`), `gandha` is the unique defining mark (`lakṣaṇa`) of the `pṛthivī` tattva, celebrated in Bhagavadgītā 7.9: `puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛthivyāṃ ca` ('I am the pure, sacred fragrance within the earth').

lakshana_deva: स्पृश्यते अनुभूयते त्वगिन्द्रियेण इति स्पर्शः । त्वगिन्द्रियमात्रग्राह्यो गुणः स्पर्शः स च त्रिविधः शीतोष्णानुष्णाशीतभेदात् ॥
lakshana_iast: spṛśyate anubhūyate tvagindriyeṇa iti sparśaḥ | tvagindriyamātragrāhyo guṇaḥ sparśaḥ sa ca trividhaḥ śītoṣṇānuṣṇāśītabhedāt ||
meaning_short: Touch or tactile quality — the sensible property perceived solely through the skin, as well as the twenty-five stop-consonants of Sanskrit phonology.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ghañ` from √spṛś ('saṃsparśane' — to touch, make direct contact), `sparśa` bridges natural philosophy and grammar. In Nyāya-Padārtha ontology (TS 27), `sparśa` is threefold across the elements: `śīta` (cool in water), `uṣṇa` (hot in fire), and `anuṣṇāśīta` (temperate in earth and air). Simultaneously in Pāṇinian Śikṣā (`kādayo māvasānāḥ sparśāḥ`), the twenty-five consonants from `ka` to `ma` are called `sparśa` ('plosives/stops') because the tongue makes full articulatory contact with palate, roof, teeth, or lips.

lakshana_deva: रज्यते चित्तमनेन इति रागः । योऽसौ ध्वनिविशेषस्तु स्वरवर्णविभूषितः रञ्जको जनचित्तानां स च राग उदाहृतः ॥
lakshana_iast: rajyate cittam anena iti rāgaḥ | yo 'sau dhvaniviśeṣas tu svaravarṇavibhūṣitaḥ rañjako janacittānāṃ sa ca rāga udāhṛtaḥ ||
meaning_short: Melodic mode (`rāga`), rich crimson hue, or emotional attachment — that which colors and captivates the human heart.
meaning_deep: Derived with `-ghañ` from √rañj ('rāge' — to dye, color, kindle emotion, charm), `rāga` exhibits a luminous semantic unity across Amarakośa (Nānārthavarga 3.3.26: `rāgo 'nurāge mātsarye lohitādau` and musicology). Visually it means glowing color (especially dawn-red `aruṇa-rāga`); psychologically it means passionate attachment (`rāga-dveṣa`, BG 2.64) or loving devotion (`bhagavad-anurāga`); and in Mataṅga's *Bṛhaddēśī* (280), a `rāga` is that living melodic framework adorned with `svaras` and `varṇas` which colors (`rañjayati`) listeners' minds with aesthetic delight.

meaning_short: Musical rhythm or cyclic time-measure — the ordered temporal foundation upon which song, instrumental play, and dance stand.
meaning_deep: Derived from √tal ('pratiṣṭhāyām' — providing firm structural grounding, also naming the palm of the hand `karatala` that claps the beat and the palmyra palm whose leaves form `tālapatra` manuscripts), Amarasimha defines `tāla` with crystalline precision in Amarakośa 1.7.9: `tālaḥ kālakriyāmānaṃ layaḥ sāmyam` — '`tāla` is the exact measure of time-intervals in performance, while `laya` is evenness of tempo'. Classical musicology reveres `śruti` (intonation) as mother and `laya`/`tāla` as father (`śrutir mātā layaḥ pitā`).

lakshana_deva: दृश्यते साक्षात्क्रियते तत्त्वमनेन इति दर्शनम् । आत्मा वा अरे द्रष्टव्यः श्रोतव्यो मन्तव्यो निदिध्यासितव्यः ॥
lakshana_iast: dṛśyate sākṣātkriyate tattvam anena iti darśanam | ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ ||
meaning_short: Vision or philosophical system — both direct sight (including sacred beholding of the Divine) and a rigorous school of inquiry that leads to direct insight into reality.
meaning_deep: Formed instrumentally with `-lyuṭ` (Pāṇini 3.3.115: `dṛśyate tattvam anena`) from √dṛśir ('prekṣaṇe' — to see directly), `darśana` reveals why Indian philosophy is never mere abstract speculation: its telos is transformative vision (`tattva-darśana` / `aparokṣa-darśana`, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.5 `ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ`). Amarakośa (Nānārthavarga) notes its meanings of eye, mirror, discernment, sacred `śāstra`, and beholding a deity or saint, crowned in Śrī Madhvācārya's tradition as `Pūrṇaprajña-darśana` (`Tattvavāda`).

lakshana_deva: सिद्धोऽन्तो निश्चयो यस्मिन् स सिद्धान्तः । प्रमाणैरर्थपरीक्षणं न्यायः तन्त्राभ्युपगमः सिद्धान्तः ॥

meaning_short: An established conclusion (`rāddhānta`) — a philosophical or scientific truth firmly demonstrated by valid `pramāṇas` after refuting counter-arguments.
meaning_deep: Compounded of `siddha` ('proven by valid evidence') + `anta` ('definitive conclusion', parallel to Amarakośa 1.5.5 `siddhānto rāddhāntaḥ`), `siddhānta` represents the culmination of classical Sanskrit dialectical method: first stating the prima facie objection (`pūrvapakṣa`), testing it with critical evidence (`khaṇḍana` / `parīkṣā`), and arriving at the unassailable `uttarapakṣa` or `siddhānta` (Gautama's *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.26–27). In astronomy too (*Sūryasiddhānta*), it denotes a mathematically proven treatise.

lakshana_deva: अभ्यस्यते पुनः पुनरनुष्ठीयते इति अभ्यासः । तत्र स्थितौ यत्नोऽभ्यासः अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते ॥
lakshana_iast: abhyasyate punaḥ punar anuṣṭhīyate iti abhyāsaḥ | tatra sthitau yatno 'bhyāsaḥ abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate ||
meaning_short: Sustained practice or disciplined repetition — earnest, uninterrupted effort that transforms initial learning into effortless mastery and mental steadiness.
meaning_deep: Derived from `abhi` + √asu ('kṣepaṇe' — applying the mind repeatedly toward a chosen discipline; `-ghañ`), `abhyāsa` denotes scholarly recitation (`svādhyāya-abhyāsa`), artistic training, grammatical reduplication (Pāṇini 6.1.4), and spiritual cultivation. lakshana_deva: परित ईक्ष्यते तत्त्वं निर्णीयते अनया इति परीक्षा । प्रतिज्ञाहेतूदाहरणोपनयनिगमनानि पञ्चावयवैः परीक्षणं परीक्षा ॥
lakshana_iast: parita īkṣyate tattvaṃ nirṇīyate anayā iti parīkṣā | pratijñāhetūdāharaṇopanayanigamanāni pañcāvayavaiḥ parīkṣaṇaṃ parīkṣā ||
meaning_short: Critical examination or testing — thorough, all-round scrutiny (`paritaḥ īkṣaṇam`) that separates genuine truth or merit from counterfeit appearance.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-aṅ` + `-ṭāp` (Pāṇini 3.3.104) from `pari` ('all around, from every angle') + √īkṣ ('darśane' — to inspect rigorously), `parīkṣā` is the third pillar of Vātsyāyana's *Nyāyabhāṣya* method: `uddeśa` (enumeration), `lakṣaṇa` (definition), and `parīkṣā` (critical verification whether the definition withstands counterexamples). Kālidāsa (*Mālavikāgnimitra* 1.2: `santaḥ parīkṣyānyatarad bhajante`) praises wise critics who judge nothing blindly by age or novelty, choosing excellence only after independent `parīkṣā`.

meaning_short: Simile or illuminating comparison — perceiving charming shared excellence (`sādharmya`) between two distinct entities (`upameya` and `upamāna`).
meaning_deep: Derived from `upa` ('near, alongside') + √mā ('māne' — to measure together; Pāṇini 3.3.106 `ātacca upasarge`), `upamā` is revered since Yāska's *Nirukta* (3.13–18) and Mammaṭa's *Kāvyaprakāśa* (10.1: `sādharmyam upamā bhede`) as the queen and fountainhead of all poetic figures (`alaṅkāra-śiroratnam`), celebrated in the adage `upamā kālidāsasya`. meaning_short: Dialogue or earnest conversation — constructive, truth-seeking discourse between interlocutors, as well as concord among independent testimonies.

meaning_deep: Yāska (Nirukta 4.5: `atithir abhyatīto gṛhān bhavati` — one who journeys to houses) and Manusmṛti 3.102 (`ekarātraṃ tu nivasann atithir brāhmaṇaḥ smṛtaḥ, anityaṃ hi sthito yasmāt tasmād atithir ucyate` — 'not staying permanently, arriving without fixed `tithi`') explain `atithi`. lakshana_iast: ācāraṃ grāhayati ācinoty arthān buddhiṃ veti ācāryaḥ | upanīya tu yaḥ śiṣyaṃ vedam adhyāpayed dvijaḥ sakalpaṃ sarahasyaṃ ca tam ācāryaṃ pracakṣate ||
meaning_short: A preceptor or master teacher — one who gathers scriptural meanings, embodies righteous conduct (`ācāra`) in his own life, and imparts liberating wisdom to students.
meaning_deep: Yāska's celebrated threefold etymology in Nirukta 1.4 (`ācāryaḥ kasmāt? ācāraṃ grāhayati, ācinoty arthān, ācinoti buddhim iti vā`) defines the true `ācārya`: (1) he instills ethical character (`ācāra`) by living it himself, (2) he systematically synthesizes scriptural meanings (`arthān ācinoti`), and (3) he cultivates the student's intellect (`buddhim ācinoti`). lakshana_iast: rañjayati prajāṃ dharmeṇa rājate vā iti rājā | rājā prakṛtirañjanāt rājā rāṭ pārthivakṣmābhṛn nṛpabhūpamahīkṣitaḥ ||
meaning_short: A king or sovereign (`nṛpa`) — a ruler whose legitimacy rests upon gladdening and protecting citizens (`prajā-rañjana`) in accordance with dharma.
meaning_deep: While grammatically formed via Uṇādi 1.156 (`rājeḥ kanin`) from √rājṛ ('dīptau' — shining with sovereign majesty, cognate with Latin *rēx*), Kālidāsa (*Raghuvaṃśa* 4.12) and Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 59.125: `rājā prakṛtirañjanāt`) enshrine the deeper ethical *nirukti* from √rañj: a ruler is truly a `rājā` only insofar as he gladdens (`rañjayati`) his people through just governance, just as `nṛpa` (`nṝn pāti`) means 'protector of human beings'. Amarakośa opens Kṣatriyavarga (2.8.1–2) with `rājan`, `rāṭ`, `pārthiva`, `kṣmābhṛt`, `nṛpa`, `bhūpa`, and `mahīkṣit`, echoed in Kauṭilya's *Arthaśāstra* 1.19.34: `prajāsukhe sukhaṃ rājñaḥ`.

lakshana_iast: prajāyate iti prajā | prajā syāt santatau jane prajāsukhe sukhaṃ rājñaḥ prajānāṃ ca hite hitam ||
meaning_short: The people, citizens of a commonwealth, or filial progeny — the living community whose welfare is the supreme purpose of governance.
meaning_deep: Formed with suffix `-ḍa` + `-ṭāp` (Pāṇini 3.2.99 / 3.3.100 on `pra` + √jan 'prādurbhāve'), `prajā` unites familial and civic life in Amarakośa (Nānārthavarga 3.3.32: `prajā syāt santatau jane`) — signifying both children (`santati`) and citizens (`jana` / `prakṛti`). meaning_short: An assembly, council, or scholarly conclave (`pariṣad` / `saṃsad`) — a deliberative gathering where wise elders uphold truth and justice.
meaning_deep: Explained etymologically as `saha bhānti asyām` ('wherein learned peers shine together in reasoned deliberation', `sa` + √bhā), `sabhā` (already paired with `samiti` in Ṛgveda 10.191 and Atharvaveda 7.12 as twin pillars of civic concord) is grouped in Amarakośa (Brahmavarga 2.7.15) with `samāja`, `saṃsad` (modern Sanskrit for parliament), `pariṣad`, `goṣṭhī`, and `samiti`. meaning_deep: Formed with `-ghañ` from √diś ('atisarjanapradarśanayoḥ' — pointing out or demarcating a region), `deśa` operates across two classic registers. lakshana_iast: gṛhṇāti dhānyādi parijanaṃ ca saṃvṛṇoti iti gṛham | gṛhaṃ gehodavasitaṃ veśma sadma niketanam niśāntaṃ sadanaṃ bhavanam āgāraṃ mandiraṃ ca ||
meaning_short: A house or home — the sheltered sanctuary where a family dwells, welcomes guests, and practices `gṛhastha-dharma`.

meaning_short: A task, rightful duty (`kartavya`), or produced effect — both what ought to be accomplished through effort and whatever arises from a prior cause.
meaning_deep: Formed by Pāṇini 3.1.124 (`ṛhalor ṇyat` — √kṛ + gerundive `-ṇyat` → `kārya`, 'to be done / producible'), `kārya` unites ethics and metaphysics. Ethically in Bhagavadgītā 3.19 (`tasmād asaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara`) and 16.24 (`kāryākāryavyavasthitau`), `kārya` means appointed duty performed without egoistic attachment. Ontologically in Nyāya and Tattvavāda (`prāgabhāvapratiyogi kāryam`, TS 39), an effect (`kārya`) is that which previously had prior non-existence (`prāgabhāva`) and is genuinely brought into manifestation through material (`upādāna`) and efficient (`nimitta`) causes.

lakshana_deva: उद्यम्यते प्रारभ्यते कार्यमनेनेति उद्यमः । उद्यमेन हि सिध्यन्ति कार्याणि न मनोरथैः ॥
lakshana_iast: udyamyate prārabhyate kāryam aneneti udyamaḥ | udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ ||
meaning_short: Resolute effort or enterprise (`puruṣakāra` / `utsāha`) — energetic, persevering initiative through which noble undertakings succeed.
meaning_deep: Formed from `ud` + √yam ('uparame / udyamane' — lifting oneself resolutely to the task; Pāṇini 3.3.57 `-ap`), `udyama` is grouped in Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.25 & Sāmānya) with `utsāha` ('buoyant energy', root-bhāva of heroic `vīra-rasa`), `udyoga`, `adhyavasāya`, and `pauruṣa` / `puruṣakāra`. Pañcatantra / Hitopadeśa (Prastāvanā 36) immortalizes its pragmatic ethic: `udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ, na hi suptasya siṃhasya praviśanti mukhe mṛgāḥ` — 'by diligent effort alone are tasks accomplished, never by mere wishful thinking; deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion!'

lakshana_deva: सेव्यते आराध्यते गुरुर्जनो भगवान्वा अनया इति सेवा । शुश्रूषा परिचर्या च सेवा अर्चा च उपासना ॥
lakshana_iast: sevyate ārādhyate gurur jano bhagavān vā anayā iti sevā | śuśrūṣā paricaryā ca sevā arcā ca upāsanā ||
meaning_short: Selfless service or reverent attendance (`śuśrūṣā` / `paricaryā`) — devoted care offered to elders, teachers, fellow beings, and the Supreme Lord.
meaning_deep: Derived from √ṣevṛ ('sevane' — to attend upon, cherish, honor) with `-aṅ` + `-ṭāp` (Pāṇini 3.3.104), `sevā` is paired in Amarakośa (Brahmavarga 2.7.35 & Śūdravarga 2.10.17) with `śuśrūṣā` (desiderative of √śru — 'attentive eagerness to listen and serve'), `paricaryā`, and `upāsanā`. Bhagavadgītā 4.34 (`tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā`) unites `sevā` directly with philosophical inquiry, and in Śrī Madhvācārya's *Tattvavāda* (`tatkarmākaraṇaṃ... sevā`), performing one's civic and compassionate duties (`paropakāra`) as loving tribute (`bhagavat-pūjā`) sanctifies all action.

lakshana_deva: दीयते स्वस्वत्वनिवृत्तिपूर्वकं परस्वत्वापादनमनेनेति दानम् । दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेऽनुपकारिणे देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्त्विकं स्मृतम् ॥
lakshana_iast: dīyate svasvatvanivṛttipūrvakaṃ parasvatvāpādanam aneneti dānam | dātavyam iti yad dānaṃ dīyate 'nupakāriṇe deśe kāle ca pātre ca tad dānaṃ sāttvikaṃ smṛtam ||
meaning_short: Generosity or charitable giving — wholeheartedly relinquishing one's own claim to bestow a gift upon another without expectation of return.
meaning_deep: Derived from √dā ('dāne' — to give; `-lyuṭ`), `dāna` (`tyāga`, `vihāpita`, `utsarga` in Amarakośa 2.7.29) is defined with juridical precision in Dharmaśāstra as `svasvatvanivṛttipūrvaka-parasvatvāpādanam` — extinguishing egoistic ownership so another becomes rightful owner. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.3 (`dāmyata, datta, dayadhvam`) enshrining Prajāpati's threefold thunder-syllable `Da-Da-Da`, and Bhagavadgītā 17.20 (`dātavyam iti yad dānaṃ...`) exalt `sāttvika-dāna` — giving food (`annadāna`), knowledge (`vidyādāna`), and safety (`abhayadāna`) purely out of duty at the right place, time, and worthy need.

english_glosses: non-harming; non-violence; harmlessness; reverence for life
phonetic_aliases: ahimsa; adroha; anrishamsya; non-violence; non-harming
lakshana_deva: सर्वथा सर्वदा सर्वभूतानामनभिद्रोहोऽहिंसा । अहिंसा परमो धर्मः मनसा वाचा कर्मणा च ॥
lakshana_iast: sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidroho 'hiṃsā | ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ manasā vācā karmaṇā ca ||
meaning_short: Non-harming — refraining in thought, word, and deed from inflicting malice or injury upon any living creature.
meaning_deep: Formed with privative `nañ` (`a-`) + `hiṃsā` (from √hiṃs 'hiṃsāyām' — injury, malice), Vyāsa's *Yogabhāṣya* on Yogasūtra 2.30 (`tatrāhiṃsā sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ`) crowns `ahiṃsā` as the root-foundation of all other ethical vows (`yama-niyamāḥ`), because truth, honesty, and self-restraint exist to perfect harmlessness. Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana Parva 115.25: `ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ`), Bhagavadgītā 16.2 (`ahiṃsā satyam akrodhaḥ`), and Śrī Madhvācārya's substitution of flour-effigies (`piṣṭa-paśu`) in place of animal injury embody this compassionate ideal.

english_glosses: compassion; mercy; tenderness; active sympathy

lakshana_deva: दयते रक्षति परदुःखं प्रमार्ष्टि अनयेति दया । कारुण्यं करुणा घृणा कृपा दयानुकम्पा स्यात् परदुःखप्रहाणेच्छा दया ॥
lakshana_iast: dayate rakṣati paraduḥkhaṃ pramārṣṭi anayeti dayā | kāruṇyaṃ karuṇā ghṛṇā kṛpā dayānukampā syāt paraduḥkhaprahāṇecchā dayā ||
meaning_short: Compassion or mercy (`karuṇā` / `kṛpā`) — the selfless impulse of the heart to relieve the suffering of others without expectation of reward.
meaning_deep: Derived from first-gaṇa Ātmanepada √day ('dānagatirakṣaṇahiṃsādāneṣu' — `dayate`, to protect, share, and shield the vulnerable; Pāṇini 3.3.104 `-aṅ`), `dayā` is grouped in Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.18) with `kāruṇya`, `karuṇā`, `kṛpā`, and `anukampā` ('trembling in empathy alongside another's pain'). Classical Vedāntic ethics defines `dayā` precisely as `svārthānapekṣa-paraduḥkha-prahāṇecchā` ('the uncalculating desire to remove another's sorrow'), celebrated in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.2.3 (`dayadhvam`), Bhagavadgītā 16.2 (`dayā bhūteṣu`), and Tattvavāda's teaching that supreme `bhagavat-kṛpā` (`prasāda`) unlocks liberation.

lakshana_deva: मित्रस्य भावः कर्म वा मैत्री । मैत्रीकरुणामुदितोपेक्षणां सुखदुःखपुण्यापुण्यविषयाणां भावनातश्चित्तप्रसादनम् ॥
lakshana_iast: mitrasya bhāvaḥ karma vā maitrī | maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāṇāṃ sukhaduḥkhapuṇyāpuṇyaviṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaś cittaprasādanam ||
meaning_short: Active friendliness or universal benevolence — the warm disposition of a true friend (`mitra`) wishing well-being and happiness to all.
meaning_deep: Formed with taddhita `-aṇ` + `-ṅīp` from `mitra` (`mitrasya bhāvaḥ`), `maitrī` (`sauhārda`, `sakhya`) stands first among Patañjali's four luminous heart-purifiers in *Yogasūtra* 1.33: cultivating warm `maitrī` toward the happy (curing envy), `karuṇā` toward the sorrowing, `muditā` (gladness) toward the virtuous, and `upekṣā` (equanimity) toward the erring brings serene lucidity (`citta-prasādana`). Equally, Bhagavadgītā 12.13 opens its portrait of the devotee dearest to Kṛṣṇa with `adveṣṭā sarvabhūtānāṃ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca` — free from ill-will toward any creature, ever friendly and compassionate.

english_glosses: forgiveness; forbearance; patience; earth
phonetic_aliases: kshama; ksama; titiksha-kshama; kshanti; marsha; forgiveness; forbearance; patience
lakshana_deva: क्षमते सहतेऽपराधं क्रोधं च संहरति अनयेति क्षमा । क्षमा तितिक्षा क्षान्तिश्च क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम् ॥
lakshana_iast: kṣamate sahate 'parādhaṃ krodhaṃ ca saṃharati anayeti kṣamā | kṣamā titikṣā kṣāntiś ca kṣamā vīrasya bhūṣaṇam ||
meaning_short: Forgiveness or noble forbearance (`kṣānti`) — unruffled composure of mind that pardons offense even when fully capable of retaliation.
meaning_deep: Derived from √kṣamūṣ ('sahane' — `kṣamate`, to bear patiently, forgive; Pāṇini 3.3.104 `-aṅ`), `kṣamā` in Amarakośa (1.7.26 & 2.1.3) names both the virtue of forgiveness (`kṣānti`, `titikṣā`) and Mother Earth herself (`kṣamā` = `pṛthivī`), who patiently bears even those who dig and strike her. Vidura-nīti (*Mahābhārata* 5.33.47: `kṣamā śastram akartṛkam` — 'in the hand of one armed with forgiveness, what harm can the wicked do?') and `kṣamā vīrasya bhūṣaṇam` affirm that forgiveness is not weakness, but the supreme ornament of inner strength (`BG 10.34, 16.3`).

phonetic_aliases: shanti; santi; prashanti; upashama; nirvriti; peace; tranquility
lakshana_deva: शाम्यति उपरमति तापत्रयमनयेति शान्तिः । अशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम् श्रद्धावान् लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥
lakshana_iast: śāmyati uparamati tāpatrayam anayeti śāntiḥ | aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham śraddhāvān labhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntim acireṇādhigacchati ||
meaning_short: Peace or deep inner serenity (`praśānti`) — the stilling of agitation and threefold sorrow (`ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika`).
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ktin` (Pāṇini 3.3.94, lengthening `a` to `ā` by 6.4.15 *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*) from fourth-gaṇa √śamu ('upaśame' — `śāmyati`, to grow calm and still), `śānti` (`śama`, `upaśama`) frames every Vedic Upaniṣad through the thrice-uttered benediction `Oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ` — invoking harmony across inner mind, surrounding creatures, and cosmic forces. Bhagavadgītā 2.66 (`aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham` — 'without inner peace, how can there be happiness?') and 4.39 (`parāṃ śāntim`) show that lasting peace flowers from sense-mastery, `jñāna`, and resting in Paramātman (`śāntir āpnoti mām`, BG 5.29).

english_glosses: bliss; joy; felicity; spiritual beatitude
phonetic_aliases: ananda; harsha; pramoda; mud; moda; ullasa; joy; bliss
lakshana_deva: आसमन्तान्नन्दति मोदतेऽनेन इति आनन्दः । मुत्प्रीतिः प्रमदो हर्षः प्रमोदामोदसम्मदाः आनन्दो ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् ॥
lakshana_iast: āsamantān nandati modate 'nena iti ānandaḥ | mut prītiḥ pramado harṣaḥ pramodāmodasammadāḥ ānando brahmeti vyajānāt ||
meaning_short: Joy or plenary bliss — radiant delight of heart, ascending in Upaniṣadic hierarchy to the infinite, unconditioned Bliss of Brahman.
meaning_deep: Derived from `ā` ('completely, on every side') + √ṭunadi ('samṛddhau' — `nandati`, to rejoice in fullness; `-ghañ`), `ānanda` is grouped in Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.23) with `mud`, `prīti`, `pramada`, `harṣa`, `pramoda`, `āmoda`, and `sammada`. Taittirīya Upaniṣad's *Ānandavallī* (2.8 & 3.6: `ānando brahmeti vyajānāt`) unfolds the celebrated `ānanda-tāratamya` — a hundredfold geometric scale ascending from human joy through celestial sages up to Four-faced Brahmā and culminating in the measureless, self-subsistent `Ānanda` of Bhagavān Viṣṇu, expounded by Śrī Madhvācārya (*Ānandatīrtha*) to prove graded intrinsic bliss even in `mokṣa`.

lakshana_deva: स्निह्यति द्रवीभवति चित्तमनेन इति स्नेहः । चूर्णादिपिण्डीभावहेतुर्गुणः स्नेहः प्रेमा ना प्रियता हार्दं प्रेम स्नेहश्च ॥
lakshana_iast: snihyati dravībhavati cittam anena iti snehaḥ | cūrṇādipiṇḍībhāvahetur guṇaḥ snehaḥ premā nā priyatā hārdaṃ prema snehaś ca ||
meaning_short: Affection or tender love (`preman` / `hārda`) — the warm quality that binds hearts together, mirroring physical cohesion and lamp-oil.
meaning_deep: Derived with `-ghañ` from fourth-gaṇa √ṣṇih ('prītau' — `snihyati`, to feel tender love, be smooth/cohesive), `sneha` possesses one of Sanskrit's most poetic double meanings: in Nyāya physics (`TS 30`), `sneha` is the cohesive viscidity of water/oil that binds dry flour into a single ball (`piṇḍībhāvahetu`) and fuels a glowing `dīpa`; in human life (Amarakośa 1.7.28: `premā priyatā hārdaṃ prema snehaḥ`), `sneha` is heartfelt affection (`vātsalya`, `sakhya`, `anurāga`) that melts isolation and binds souls in enduring care — crowned in Śrī Madhvācārya's *Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* (1.86) where `bhakti` itself is defined as `māhātmyajñānapūrvakas tu sudṛḍhaḥ sarvato 'dhikaḥ snehaḥ`.

english_glosses: faith; reverent trust; earnest conviction; sincerity

lakshana_deva: श्रत् सत्यं दधाति धारयति चित्तमनया इति श्रद्धा । आस्तिक्यबुद्धिः श्रद्धा श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः ॥
lakshana_iast: śrat satyaṃ dadhāti dhārayati cittam anayā iti śraddhā | āstikyabuddhiḥ śraddhā śraddhāmayo 'yaṃ puruṣo yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ ||
meaning_short: Reverent faith or earnest trust — placing one's heart upon truth (`śrat` + √dhā), uniting intellectual respect for valid `śāstra` with wholehearted sincerity.
meaning_deep: Yāska (Nirukta 9.30: `śraddhā śraddadhānāt`, `śrat` = 'satya / truth' in Nighaṇṭu 3.10 + √dhā 'dhāraṇe' + `-aṅ` by Pāṇini 3.3.106, directly cognate with Latin *crēdō* 'I place my heart/trust') reveals that Vedic `śraddhā` (hymned in RV 10.151) is never blind credulity, but `āstikya-buddhi` — serene, receptive confidence in trustworthy guru-śāstra and moral law, likened in *Yogabhāṣya* 1.20 (`sā hi jananīva kalyāṇī yoginaṃ pāti`) to a loving mother protecting the seeker. Bhagavadgītā 17.3 declares `śraddhāmayo 'yaṃ puruṣo yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ` — a person is shaped by the quality of their deepest conviction.

english_glosses: austerity; disciplined ardor; contemplative focus; penance
phonetic_aliases: tapas; tapah; tapasya; vrata; samyama; austerity; discipline
lakshana_deva: तपति दहति कल्मषमालोचयति तत्त्वं वानेन इति तपः । मनसश्चेन्द्रियाणां च ह्यैकाग्र्यं परमं तपः ॥
lakshana_iast: tapati dahati kalmaṣam ālocayati tattvaṃ vānena iti tapaḥ | manasaś cendriyāṇāṃ ca hy aikāgryaṃ paramaṃ tapaḥ ||
meaning_short: Disciplined ardor or spiritual austerity — focused inner heat that refines away dross and gathers mind and senses into one-pointed clarity.
meaning_deep: Derived with `-asun` from √tap ('santāpe / aiśvarye / ālocane' — glowing with purifying ardor and deep reflection, as in Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9 `yasya jñānamayaṃ tapaḥ`, where Paramātman's `tapas` is pure effortless omniscience), `tapas` in human ethics never means self-torture (expressly rejected as `āsura` in BG 17.19). Rather, Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 250.4: `manasaś cendriyāṇāṃ ca hy aikāgryaṃ paramaṃ tapaḥ`) and Bhagavadgītā 17.14–16 define true `tapas` across three planes: bodily (`śārīra` — purity, `ahiṃsā`, honoring elders), vocal (`vāṅmaya` — truthful, gentle speech), and mental (`mānasa` — serenity, silence, and guileless integrity).

english_glosses: sacrifice; worship; sacred offering; consecrated service
phonetic_aliases: yajna; yagna; makha; kratu; adhvara; savana; sacrifice; worship
lakshana_deva: इज्यते पूज्यते परमात्मा देवाश्च अनेन इति यज्ञः । यज्ञः सप्ततन्तुर्मखः क्रतुरध्वरः यज्ञो वै विष्णुः ॥
lakshana_iast: ijyate pūjyate paramātmā devāś ca anena iti yajñaḥ | yajñaḥ saptatantur makhaḥ kratur adhvaraḥ yajño vai viṣṇuḥ ||
meaning_short: Sacred worship or sacrificial offering (`adhvara`) — any consecrated act of devotion, study, or selfless service offered unto the Supreme.
meaning_deep: Formed by Pāṇini 3.3.90 (`yajayācayatavicchapraccharakṣo naṅ` — √yaj 'devapūjāsaṅgatikaraṇadāneṣu' + `-naṅ` → `yajña`), Dhātupāṭha's own three root-meanings capture the heart of `yajña`: (1) `devapūjā` — reverent worship, (2) `saṅgatikaraṇa` — uniting community and cosmos in harmony, and (3) `dāna` — generous offering. Amarakośa (Brahmavarga 2.7.13) pairs `yajña` with `saptatantu`, `makha`, `kratu`, and `adhvara` (Yāska, Nirukta 1.8: `a-dhvara` = 'devoid of violence/harm'). Crowned by Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's `yajño vai viṣṇuḥ` and Bhagavadgītā 4.24–33 (`jñānayajña`), every noble act offered without selfishness (`yajñārthāt karmaṇaḥ`, BG 3.9) liberates rather than binds.

english_glosses: courage; fortitude; composure; steadfastness

lakshana_deva: धीरस्य भावः धैर्यम् । विकारहेतौ सति विक्रियन्ते येषां न चेतांसि त एव धीराः ॥
lakshana_iast: dhīrasya bhāvaḥ dhairyam | vikārahetau sati vikriyante yeṣāṃ na cetāṃsi ta eva dhīrāḥ ||
meaning_short: Courage, fortitude, or unshaken composure (`dhṛti`) — steadiness of heart that remains unperturbed even amidst severe provocation or peril.
meaning_deep: Formed with abstract suffix `-ṣyañ` (Pāṇini 5.1.124) from `dhīra` ('grounded in discerning `dhī` and unshakable resolve'), `dhairya` (`dhṛti` in BG 18.33) is luminously defined by Kālidāsa in *Kumārasambhava* 1.59: `vikārahetau sati vikriyante yeṣāṃ na cetāṃsi ta eva dhīrāḥ` — 'they alone are truly `dhīra` whose minds do not waver even when every cause for perturbation stands before them.' Bhartṛhari (*Nītiśataka* 83) adds that great souls (`mahātmanaḥ`) never deviate from the path of justice whether praised or censured, whether fortune comes or departs (`nyāyyāt pathaḥ pravicalanti padaṃ na dhīrāḥ`).

phonetic_aliases: vinaya; namrata; prashraya; sushikshana; humility; modesty; courtesy
lakshana_deva: विनीयते शिक्ष्यते इन्द्रियग्रामोऽनेन इति विनयः । विद्या ददाति विनयं विनयाद्याति पात्रताम् विद्याविनयसम्पन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि ॥
lakshana_iast: vinīyate śikṣyate indriyagrāmo 'nena iti vinayaḥ | vidyā dadāti vinayaṃ vinayād yāti pātratām vidyāvinayasampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini ||
meaning_short: Humility, courtesy, and refined self-discipline (`praśraya`) — the graceful absence of arrogance that adorns genuine learning.
meaning_deep: Derived with `-ac` (Pāṇini 3.3.56) from `vi` + √nīñ ('prāpaṇe / śikṣaṇe' — guiding the senses and ego into cultured poise), `vinaya` (`praśraya` in Amarakośa 3.3.149) unites personal humility with educated refinement. Kauṭilya (*Arthaśāstra* 1.5) makes `indriya-jaya` the root of royal `vinaya`, Hitopadeśa 0.6 (`vidyā dadāti vinayam`) makes `vinaya` the first fruit proving whether education has truly taken root (`phalino namrās taravaḥ` — fruit-laden boughs bow low), and Bhagavadgītā 5.18 pairs `vidyā` and `vinaya` (`vidyāvinayasampanne`) as inseparable twin virtues of the sage.

lakshana_deva: शील्यतेऽभ्यस्यते सद्भिरिति शीलम् । शीलं स्वभावे सद्वृत्ते शीलं परं भूषणम् ॥
lakshana_iast: śīlyate 'bhyasyate sadbhir iti śīlam | śīlaṃ svabhāve sadvṛtte śīlaṃ paraṃ bhūṣaṇam ||
meaning_short: Noble character or moral integrity (`sad-vṛtta` / `sadācāra`) — habitual excellence of disposition practiced consistently in public and private.
meaning_deep: Derived from √śīl ('samādhau / upadhāraṇe' — cultivated until uprightness becomes effortless second nature), `śīla` is defined concisely in Amarakośa (Nānārthavarga 3.3.199 & 1.7.32): `śīlaṃ svabhāve sadvṛtte` — innate disposition and upright conduct. Mahābhārata (Udyogaparva & Śāntiparva 124) lists thirteen hallmarks of `śīla` — truthfulness, self-restraint, non-malice, modesty, generosity, and gratitude — while Bhartṛhari (*Nītiśataka* 82) concludes his enumeration of human virtues with the ringing verdict: `śīlaṃ paraṃ bhūṣaṇam` ('noble character is the supreme ornament of a human being').

lakshana_deva: सत्क्रियते पूज्यतेऽतिथिर्गुणवान्वानेन इति सत्कारः । अर्घ्यादिभिः पूजनमादरश्च सत्कारः तृणानि भूमिरुदकं वाक्चतुर्थी च सूनृता ॥
lakshana_iast: satkriyate pūjyate 'tithir guṇavān vānena iti satkāraḥ | arghyādibhiḥ pūjanam ādaraś ca satkāraḥ tṛṇāni bhūmir udakaṃ vāk caturthī ca sūnṛtā ||
meaning_short: Gracious hospitality or honor (`ādara` / `saparyā`) — welcoming guests, elders, and merit with sincere respect and kindness.
meaning_deep: Formed by Pāṇini 1.4.63 (`ādaranādarayoḥ sadasatī` — `sat` and `asat` as `gati` prefixes before √kṛ: `sat` + `kāra` = 'honoring graciously', opposite of `asatkāra` = disrespect), `satkāra` is paired in Amarakośa (2.7.34–35) with `arghya`, `pādya`, `saparyā`, and `ādara`. Manusmṛti 3.101 (`tṛṇāni bhūmir udakaṃ vāk caturthī ca sūnṛtā, etāny api satāṃ gehe nocchidyante kadācana`) teaches that even when material means are modest, true `satkāra` never fails in a noble home: a mat to sit on, space to rest, cool water, and fourth — a warm, truthful word of welcome (`sūnṛtā vāk`).

lakshana_deva: कीर्त्यते प्रशस्यते सद्भिर्देशान्तरेष्वपि इति कीर्तिः । यशः कीर्तिः समज्ञा च कीर्तिर्यस्य स जीवति ॥
lakshana_iast: kīrtyate praśasyate sadbhir deśāntareṣv api iti kīrtiḥ | yaśaḥ kīrtiḥ samajñā ca kīrtir yasya sa jīvati ||
meaning_short: Unsullied renown or noble reputation (`yaśas`) — the fragrant remembrance earned by righteous deeds, generosity, and scholarship.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ktin` from tenth-gaṇa √kṝt ('saṃśabdane' — `kīrtayati`, to celebrate, proclaim with praise), `kīrti` is grouped in Amarakośa (Śabdādivarga 1.6.11) with `yaśas` and `samajñā` (later poetics subtly distinguishing `kīrti` born of generosity/piety from `yaśas` born of valor, both pure moonlight-white in poetic convention). Exalted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Bhagavadgītā 10.34 (`kīrtiḥ śrīr vāk ca nārīṇām`) and echoed in Subhāṣita wisdom (`sa jīvati guṇā yasya, kīrtir yasya sa jīvati`), spotless `kīrti-kāya` ('the body of good renown', Bhartṛhari *Nītiśataka* 24) outlives mortal age and death.

lakshana_deva: जयति उत्कर्षं प्राप्नोति धर्मेणेति जयः । यतो धर्मस्ततो जयः यत्र योगेश्वरः कृष्णो यत्र पार्थो धनुर्धरः तत्र श्रीर्विजयो भूतिर्ध्रुवा नीतिर्मतिर्मम ॥
lakshana_iast: jayati utkarṣaṃ prāpnoti dharmeṇeti jayaḥ | yato dharmas tato jayaḥ yatra yogeśvaraḥ kṛṣṇo yatra pārtho dhanurdharaḥ tatra śrīr vijayo bhūtir dhruvā nītir matir mama ||
meaning_short: Victory or righteous triumph (`vijaya`) — mastery over outer obstacles and inner passions, rooted unfailingly in dharma.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ac` (`er ac`, Pāṇini 3.3.56) from √ji ('jaye' — `jayati`, to conquer, excel), `jaya` (`vijaya`, AK 2.8.106) is the original sacred title of Vyāsa's *Mahābhārata* (`tato jayam udīrayet`), because its central teaching — expounded across Śrī Madhvācārya's *Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* and *Jayatīrtha*'s commentaries — is `yato dharmas tato jayaḥ` ('wherever Dharma stands, there stands Victory') and `satyam eva jayate` (Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.6). Bhagavadgītā closes at 18.78 uniting divine grace (`Yogeśvara Kṛṣṇa`) and resolute human effort (`dhanurdhara Pārtha`) as the infallible locus of `śrī`, `vijaya`, and `dhruvā nīti`.

lakshana_deva: मङ्गति गच्छति भद्रमनेन अघं वा अपसारयति इति मङ्गलम् । श्वःश्रेयसं शिवं भद्रं कल्याणं मङ्गलं शुभम् भावुकं भविकं भव्यं कुशलं क्षेममस्त्रियाम् ॥
lakshana_iast: maṅgati gacchati bhadram anena aghaṃ vā apasārayati iti maṅgalam | śvaḥśreyasaṃ śivaṃ bhadraṃ kalyāṇaṃ maṅgalaṃ śubham bhāvukaṃ bhavikaṃ bhavyaṃ kuśalaṃ kṣemam astriyām ||
meaning_short: Auspiciousness, holistic well-being, or benediction (`kalyāṇa` / `śubha` / `bhadra`) — whatever removes obstacles and brings enduring good.
meaning_deep: Derived via Uṇādi 5.70 (`maṅger alac`) from √maṅg ('gatau / śubhe' — advancing wholesome good), `maṅgala` inspires one of Amarakośa's most resonant verses (Svargavarga 1.4.25): `śvaḥśreyasa`, `śiva`, `bhadra`, `kalyāṇa`, `maṅgala`, `śubha`, `bhāvuka`, `bhavya`, `kuśala`, `kṣema`, and `svasti`. Every Sanskrit `śāstra` and `kāvya` opens with a `maṅgalācaraṇa` (auspicious invocation of the Supreme Lord — as in Śrī Madhvācārya's `nārāyaṇaṃ nikhilapūrṇaguṇaikadeham`) so that study and life may reach unobstructed completion (`nirvighna-parisamāpti`).

lakshana_deva: स्वतन्त्रस्य भावः स्वातन्त्र्यम् । स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता स्वरूपप्रमितप्रवृत्त्यादिलक्षणसत्तात्रैविध्ये परानपेक्षत्वं स्वातन्त्र्यम् ॥
lakshana_iast: svatantrasya bhāvaḥ svātantryam | svatantraḥ kartā svarūpapramitapravṛttyādilakṣaṇasattātraividhye parānapekṣatvaṃ svātantryam ||
meaning_short: Freedom, autonomy, or sovereign independence — in grammar and civic life, self-directed agency; in Tattvavāda metaphysics, Paramātman's unique non-dependence upon any other.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ṣyañ` (Pāṇini 5.1.124) from `svatantra` ('whose loom/governance `tantra` is one's own', celebrated in Pāṇini's agent definition 1.4.54 `svatantraḥ kartā` and Manusmṛti 4.160 `sarvaṃ paravaśaṃ duḥkhaṃ sarvam ātmavaśaṃ sukham` — 'subjugation is sorrow; self-determination is happiness'), `svātantrya` operates on two harmonized levels. Ethically and civically, a human agent possesses real moral choice (`kartṛtva`), never being an inert stone; metaphysically in Śrī Madhvācārya's *Tattvasaṅkhyāna* (`svatantram asvatantraṃ ca`), absolute `svātantrya` (`parānapekṣatva` in essence, knowledge, and power) belongs exclusively to Bhagavān Viṣṇu, who graciously empowers finite freedom.

lakshana_iast: nīyate lokaḥ sanmārgeṇa śreyaḥ prati anayā iti nītiḥ | nayo nītir nyāyaś ca daṇḍo damayatām asmi nītir asmi jigīṣatām ||
meaning_short: Ethics, moral wisdom, or principled statesmanship (`naya`) — the guiding art of right conduct that leads individuals and communities safely toward welfare.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ktin` (Pāṇini 3.3.94) from √nīñ ('prāpaṇe' — `nayati`, guiding wisely toward the good), `nīti` (`naya`) names the vast practical literature of Indian ethics and statecraft — from *Vidura-nīti*, *Pañcatantra*, *Hitopadeśa*, and *Śukranīti* (`sarvalokavyavahārasthitihetuḥ nītiḥ`) to Bhartṛhari's *Nītiśataka*. Crucially, Bhagavadgītā 10.38 (`nītir asmi jigīṣatām`) and 18.78 (`dhruvā nītiḥ`) insist that authentic `nīti` is never cynical expediency divorced from righteousness; true statesmanship is steadfast `dharma` applied with foresight and fairness (`nyāya`).

lakshana_deva: उत्सूयते हर्षोऽस्मिन्निति उत्सवः । क्षण उद्धव आनन्द उत्सवो महश्च सः उत्सवप्रियाः खलु मनुष्याः ॥
lakshana_iast: utsūyate harṣo 'sminn iti utsavaḥ | kṣaṇa uddhava ānanda utsavo mahaś ca saḥ utsavapriyāḥ khalu manuṣyāḥ ||
meaning_short: A festival or communal celebration (`maha` / `parvan`) — an auspicious occasion that brings forth collective joy, art, generosity, and sacred remembrance.
meaning_deep: Formed with `-ap` (Pāṇini 3.3.57) from `ud` + √ṣū ('prasave' — generating buoyant joy, or blossoming like a new shoot `prasava`), `utsava` is grouped in Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.36) with `kṣaṇa`, `uddhava`, and `maha`. Kālidāsa's *Abhijñānaśākuntalam* (6.2) captures human nature in a gentle four-word aphorism: `utsavapriyāḥ khalu manuṣyāḥ` — 'human beings indeed delight in festivals!' Across temple `rathotsavas`, seasonal `ṛtu-utsavas`, and scholarly gatherings, `utsava` weaves music, hospitality, and devotion into shared civic joy.

lakshana_deva: क्रीड्यते विह्रियते अनया इति क्रीडा । द्रवः केलिः परीहासो नर्म क्रीडा च लीलया लोकवत्तु लीलाकैवल्यम् ॥
lakshana_iast: krīḍyate vihriyate anayā iti krīḍā | dravaḥ keliḥ parīhāso narma krīḍā ca līlayā lokavat tu līlākaivalyam ||
meaning_short: Play, sport, or joyous pastime (`līlā` / `keli`) — spontaneous activity performed out of overflowing delight rather than external compulsion or lack.
meaning_deep: Derived from √krīḍṛ ('vihāre' — to sport, play joyfully; Pāṇini 3.3.104 `-aṅ`), `krīḍā` is grouped in Amarakośa (Nāṭyavarga 1.7.33) with `drava`, `keli`, `narma`, `khela`, and `līlā`. Beyond childhood games and athletic recreation, *Brahmasūtra* 2.1.33 (`lokavat tu līlākaivalyam`) elevates `krīḍā` / `līlā` to solve the deepest question of philosophical theology: why does an already-complete, desireless (`āptakāma`) Supreme Being create and sustain the universe? Śrī Madhvācārya's *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* explains that just as a joyous person sings or dances spontaneously from sheer overflowing bliss without needing any personal gain, Viṣṇu's cosmic governance is pure `līlā` undertaken solely for the upliftment of dependent souls.

lakshana_iast: na vidyate bhayaṃ yasmād yasmin vā tat abhayam | abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhir jñānayogavyavasthitiḥ abhayaṃ vai prāpto bhavati ||
meaning_short: Fearlessness, safety, or sanctuary from all dread — both the courageous virtue heading the divine heritage (`daivī sampat`) and the promise of protection extended to all beings.
meaning_deep: Compounded of privative `a-` + `bhaya` ('fear/peril', √bhī), `abhaya` stands as the very first virtue in Bhagavadgītā Chapter 16 (`abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhiḥ`, BG 16.1), because moral integrity, truthfulness, and compassion flourish only in a fearless heart. lakshana_deva: शृणाति दुःखं भयं च रक्षति आश्रितमिति शरणम् । शरणं गृहरक्षित्रोः सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज ॥
lakshana_iast: śṛṇāti duḥkhaṃ bhayaṃ ca rakṣati āśritam iti śaraṇam | śaraṇaṃ gṛharakṣitroḥ sarvadharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja ||
meaning_short: Refuge, protective sanctuary, or saving Protector — a sheltering home and, preeminently, He who dispels all fear and sorrow for those who seek shelter.
meaning_deep: Derived with `-lyuṭ` from √śṝ ('hiṃsāyām' — `śṛṇāti ārtim`, shattering affliction and peril before they touch the refugee), Amarasimha gives a crucial two-word rule in Amarakośa (Nānārthavarga 3.3.47): `śaraṇaṃ gṛharakṣitroḥ` — neuter `śaraṇam` signifies both a sheltering house (`gṛha`) and a living Protector (`rakṣitṛ`, retaining neuter gender even when referring directly to the Lord!). Thus in Bhagavadgītā 18.66 (`mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja`) and Viṣṇusahasranāma (`śaraṇaṃ śarma viśvaretāḥ`), Śrī Madhvācārya's Gītābhāṣya highlights Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa as the one unfailing `Śaraṇam` — Shelter, Home, and Liberator of all beings.

lakshana_deva: व्याप्तृत्वाद् विष्णुरुद्दिष्टो देशतः कालतस्तथा । गुणैश्च सर्वतः पूर्णो वेवेष्टि व्यापको हरिः ॥
lakshana_iast: vyāptṛtvād viṣṇur uddiṣṭo deśataḥ kālatas tathā | guṇaiś ca sarvataḥ pūrṇo veveṣṭi vyāpako hariḥ ||
meaning_short: Viṣṇu (from √viṣḷ 'vyāptau' — to pervade) is He who possesses plenary threefold pervasion across all space, all time, and all auspicious attributes without limit.
meaning_deep: While Avyākṛtākāśa and Prakṛti pervade space and eternal flow of time (`deśataḥ kālataḥ`), they are utterly deficient in conscious attributes (`guṇataḥ apūrṇam`). Even Mahālakṣmī, though co-extensive in space and time (`deśakālābhyām eva samavyāptā` — PS 2.2), is surpassed infinitely in quality (`guṇataḥ`). Only Viṣṇu is `deśataḥ kālato guṇataś ca aparicchinnaḥ` — unbounded in space, time, and excellence.

english_glosses: Vasudeva; indwelling shelter of all worlds
phonetic_aliases: vasudeva; vaasudeva; vasudevah; वासुदेव
lakshana_deva: वसन्ति यत्र भूतानि वस्ते सर्वं जगच्च यः । द्योतनात् क्रीडनाच्चैव वासुदेवः स ईरितः ॥
lakshana_iast: vasanti yatra bhūtāni vaste sarvaṃ jagac ca yaḥ | dyotanāt krīḍanāc caiva vāsudevaḥ sa īritaḥ ||
meaning_short: Vāsudeva is He in whom all beings dwell ('vasanti'), who envelops and shelters the cosmos ('vaste'), and who shines, sports, and bestows liberation ('deva').
meaning_deep: First of the four primal Vyūha manifestations (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha), Vāsudeva is specifically revered by Madhvācārya in MBTN 1.6 (`vāsudevanāmā babhūva nijamuktipadapradātā`) as the bestower of pristine Mokṣa, as well as Beloved Son of Vasudeva in Dvārakā.

english_glosses: Bhagavan; Lord of sixfold infinite perfection
phonetic_aliases: bhagavan; bhagavaan; bhagavat; shadguna; भगवान्
lakshana_deva: ऐश्वर्यस्य समग्रस्य वीर्यस्य यशसः श्रियः । ज्ञानवैराग्ययोश्चैव षण्णां भग इतीरणा ॥ तद्वान् भगवान् ।
lakshana_iast: aiśvaryasya samagrasya vīryasya yaśasaḥ śriyaḥ | jñānavairāgyayoś caiva ṣaṇṇāṃ bhaga itīraṇā || tadvān bhagavān |
meaning_short: Bhagavān is He who eternally possesses 'Bhaga' in plenary completeness ('samagra') — unconditioned sovereignty, valour, renown, splendour, omniscience, and detachment.
meaning_deep: Citing Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.74 and MBTN 1.24 (`ṣāḍguṇyavigrahaḥ supūrṇaguṇaikadehaḥ`), Madhvācārya underscores the word `samagrasya` (total, limitless): while exalted beings may be called 'bhagavān' figuratively, Viṣṇu alone bears the title primarily without metaphor.

english_glosses: Brahman; the Infinitely Plenary Absolute
phonetic_aliases: brahma; brahman; parabrahman; brihat; purnam; ब्रह्म
lakshana_deva: ब्रह्मशब्दश्च विष्ण्वाख्यो नान्यत्र क्वचिदिष्यते । बृहत्त्वाद् बृंहणत्वाच्च गुणपूर्णत्वतो हरिः ॥
lakshana_iast: brahmaśabdaś ca viṣṇvākhyo nānyatra kvacid iṣyate | bṛhattvād bṛṃhaṇatvāc ca guṇapūrṇatvato hariḥ ||
meaning_short: Brahman (from √bṛh 'to be vast / plenary') denotes Bhagavān Viṣṇu as infinitely replete with all auspicious attributes ('guṇa-pūrṇatva') and nourisher of all beings.
meaning_deep: In Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.1 (`brahmaśabdasya viṣṇāv eva rūḍhiḥ / mahāyogaḥ`) and Anuvyākhyāna, Madhvācārya turns Advaita's nirguṇa-brahman upside down: the very etymology of 'Brahman' (`bṛhanto hy asmin guṇāḥ`) demands infinite positive attributes (`guṇa-pūrṇatva`), never attribute-less vacuity!

english_glosses: Self; Atman; Supreme Indwelling Lord
phonetic_aliases: atma; aatma; atman; paramatma; आत्मा
lakshana_deva: आततत्वाच्च मातृत्वादात्मा हि परमो हरिः । यच्चाप्नोति यदादत्ते यच्चात्ति विषयानिह ॥
lakshana_iast: ātatatvāc ca mātṛtvād ātmā hi paramo hariḥ | yac cāpnoti yad ādatte yac cātti viṣayān iha ||
meaning_short: Ātman primarily denotes Supreme Hari because He pervades all ('ātata'), measures and fashions all ('mātṛ'), obtains all ('āpnoti'), withdraws all ('ādatte'), and enjoys auspiciousness.
meaning_deep: Whenever Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas speak of the Supreme Ātman (`aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam`, `ayam ātmā brahma`), Madhvācārya cites this classical Vedic nirukti (`ātata + mātṛ`) to show that Paramātman Hari is the chief referent (`mukhyārtha`) of 'Ātman' as the Sovereign Owner and Inner Pervader of every individual jīvātman.

english_glosses: Purusha; Supreme Person; spirit
phonetic_aliases: purusha; purusa; puman; purushottama; पुरुष
lakshana_deva: स पूर्णत्वात् पुमान्नाम पौरुषे सूक्त ईरितः । पुरि शेते इति पुरुषोऽन्तर्यामिरूपस्याख्या ॥
lakshana_iast: sa pūrṇatvāt pumān nāma pauruṣe sūkta īritaḥ | puri śete iti puruṣo'ntaryāmirūpasyākhyā ||
meaning_short: Puruṣa / Pumān denotes Bhagavān both from absolute plenitude ('pūrṇatvāt') in the Puruṣa Sūkta and from reclining as Inner Ruler within the heart-city of all beings ('puri śete').
meaning_deep: Combining Ṛgbhāṣya 1.1.5 (`sa pūrṇatvāt pumān nāma`), Muṇḍaka Bhāṣya 3.5 (`vāsudevaḥ pumān nāmā pūrṇatvāt`), and Aitareya Bhāṣya 2.2.1 (`puruṣa ity antaryāmirūpasyākhyā, puri śete iti`), Madhvācārya shows how cosmic transcendence (Pūrṇa) and intimate immanence (Antaryāmī) meet in Puruṣottama.

english_glosses: Imperishable; eternal syllable or Spirit
phonetic_aliases: akshara; aksara; aksharam; imperishable; अक्षर
lakshana_deva: अपरं त्वक्षरं या सा प्रकृतिर्जडरूपिका । अक्षरं परमं श्रीस्तु परतः परमक्षरम् ॥ वासुदेवः परानन्द इति त्रिविधमक्षरम् ।
lakshana_iast: aparaṃ tv akṣaraṃ yā sā prakṛtir jaḍarūpikā | akṣaraṃ paramaṃ śrīs tu parataḥ param akṣaram || vāsudevaḥ parānanda iti trividham akṣaram |
meaning_short: Akṣara (the Imperishable, `na kṣarati` / `aśnute`) is threefold in Vedic usage: lower insentient Prakṛti, higher sentient Śrī (Mahālakṣmī), and the Supreme Imperishable beyond the imperishable — Vāsudeva.
meaning_deep: This landmark verse in Muṇḍaka Bhāṣya 3.2 resolves every apparent contradiction across the Upaniṣads and Bhagavadgītā 15.16–18 (`kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni kūṭastho'kṣara ucyate | uttamaḥ puruṣas tv anyaḥ`): all bound souls are Kṣara (having mutable bodies), Śrī-tattva is Kūṭastha-Akṣara, and Viṣṇu is `akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ`.

english_glosses: Hari; Remover of sin and sorrow
phonetic_aliases: hari; harih; हरि
lakshana_deva: हरत्यघमशेषेण भक्तानां जन्मबन्धनम् । यज्ञभागान् हरत्यग्र्यस्तस्माद्धरिरितीरितः ॥
lakshana_iast: haraty agham aśeṣeṇa bhaktānāṃ janmabandhanam | yajñabhāgān haraty agryas tasmād dharir itīritaḥ ||
meaning_short: Hari (from √hṛ 'haraṇe') is He who completely removes the sins, sorrows, and karmic bondage of devotees, receives the foremost share of all sacrifices, and withdraws the cosmos at dissolution.
meaning_deep: Throughout Sarvamūla, 'Hari' is Madhvācārya's most beloved personal name for the Supreme (`sarvottamo harir idaṃ tu tadājñayaiva` — MBTN 1.29), uniting compassionate soteriology (removing duḥkha and pāpa) with ritual and cosmic sovereignty.

english_glosses: Krishna; All-attracting Blissful Lord
phonetic_aliases: krishna; krsna; krishnah; कृष्ण
lakshana_deva: कृषिः सत्तावाचकः शब्दो णश्च निर्वृतिवाचकः । तयोरैक्यं परं ब्रह्म कृष्ण इत्यभिधीयते ॥
lakshana_iast: kṛṣiḥ sattāvācakaḥ śabdo ṇaś ca nirvṛtivācakaḥ | tayor aikyaṃ paraṃ brahma kṛṣṇa ity abhidhīyate ||
meaning_short: 'Kṛṣ' signifies sovereign, all-attracting Being (sattā / aiśvarya) and 'ṇa' signifies supreme Bliss (nirvṛti); their indivisible unity — Parabrahman — is named Kṛṣṇa.
meaning_deep: Grounded in Mahābhārata Udyogaparva 70.5 and Madhvācārya's Gītābhāṣya / MBTN, Kṛṣṇa also draws (`karṣati`) the hearts of devotees and ploughs away (`nikṛṣati`) all sins. Through Viśeṣa, Sovereign Existence (`kṛṣ`) and Infinite Bliss (`ṇa`) are wholly identical in Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

english_glosses: Rama; Supreme Delight of yogins
phonetic_aliases: rama; raama; ramah; mularama; राम
lakshana_deva: रमन्ते योगिनोऽनन्ते नित्यानन्दे चिदात्मनि । इति रामपदेनासौ परं ब्रह्माभिधीयते ॥
lakshana_iast: ramante yogino'nante nityānande cidātmani | iti rāmapadenāsau paraṃ brahmābhidhīyate ||
meaning_short: Because realized yogis delight ('ramante') in Him — the Infinite, Eternally Blissful Consciousness — Parabrahman is celebrated by the name Rāma.
meaning_deep: In Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya (Chapters 3–9, the Rāmāyaṇa-saṅgraha) and Tantrasārasaṅgraha 1.9, Madhvācārya reveres Śrī Mūlarāma (whose ancient icon he consecrated in the Udupi/uttara sampradāya) as `nirdoṣapūrṇaguṇavigraha` — any seeming human grief in Rāmāvatāra is purely `asurāṇāṃ mohāya` (MBTN 1.37).

english_glosses: Narasimha; Man-Lion Avatara
phonetic_aliases: narasimha; nrisimha; nrusimha; नरसिंह; नृसिंह
lakshana_deva: नराणां जीवानां सिंह इव सर्वोत्तमो भयहर्ता नृहरिर्नरसिंहः ।
lakshana_iast: narāṇāṃ jīvānāṃ siṃha iva sarvottamo bhayahartā nṛharir narasiṃhaḥ |
meaning_short: Narasiṃha is both the transcendent Man-Lion Avatāra whose nails effortlessly tore apart Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the Supreme Sovereign ('siṃha') over all sentient beings ('nara'), Death unto Death.
meaning_deep: Madhvācārya opened his Viṣṇustuti with the thunderous two-verse *Nakhastuti* (`pāntv asmān puruhūtavairibalavanmātaṅgamādyadghaṭā...`), celebrating the blazing fingernails of Śrī Narasiṃha as infinite Consciousness-Power (`lakṣmīkānta-samantato'pi kalayan naivaiṣituste samam`).

english_glosses: Kapila; Sage-Avatara of liberating wisdom
phonetic_aliases: kapila; kapilah; कपिल
lakshana_deva: कपिलो भगवानजः प्रोवाच ब्रह्मणे विद्याः । कं सुखं ज्ञानं च पिलति ददातीति कपिलः ॥
lakshana_iast: kapilo bhagavān ajaḥ provāca brahmaṇe vidyāḥ | kaṃ sukhaṃ jñānaṃ ca pilati dadātīti kapilaḥ ||
meaning_short: Kapila is the unborn Jñānāvatāra of Viṣṇu who imparts bliss ('ka') and true liberating wisdom, and of golden-tawny solar radiance ('kapila-varṇa').
meaning_deep: In Ṛgbhāṣya 1.1.9 and Tantrasārasaṅgraha 1.7 ('ka' → Kapila), Madhvācārya distinguishes Bhagavān Vāsudeva-Kapila (son of Kardama and Devahūti, teacher of real theistic Sāṅkhya) from any later atheistic distortion.

english_glosses: Hamsa; Immaculate Swan-Avatara
phonetic_aliases: hamsa; hans; paramahamsa; हंस
lakshana_deva: हन्ति समस्तान् दोषान् सारं च गृह्णातीति हंसः परमात्मा । सोऽहं स एवाहमस्मीति नियामकः ॥
lakshana_iast: hanti samastān doṣān sāraṃ ca gṛhṇātīti haṃsaḥ paramātmā | so'haṃ sa evāham asmīti niyāmakaḥ ||
meaning_short: Haṃsa is the Immaculate Swan-Avatāra of Paramātman who destroys ('hanti') all blemishes and accepts only pure devotion ('sāra'), the primal Guru of the Haṃsa-sampradāya.
meaning_deep: In Yatipraṇavakalpa and Tantrasārasaṅgraha 1.10, Madhvācārya explains `Haṃsa` / `So'ham` not as jīva-brahma identity, but as meditating on He ('saḥ') who is the Unabandoned ('a-heya' → `aham`) Inner Sovereign free of every defect.

english_glosses: Sankarshana; cosmic-withdrawing Vyuha form
phonetic_aliases: sankarshana; samkarshana; vyuha; सङ्कर्षण
lakshana_deva: सङ्कर्षणश्च स बभूव पुनः सुनित्यः संहारकारणवपुः । सम्यक् कर्षति जगदिति सङ्कर्षणः ॥
lakshana_iast: saṅkarṣaṇaś ca sa babhūva punaḥ sunityaḥ saṃhārakāraṇavapuḥ | samyak karṣati jagad iti saṅkarṣaṇaḥ ||
meaning_short: Saṅkarṣaṇa is the second eternal Vyūha form of Bhagavān who draws ('saṅkarṣati') the cosmos back into Himself during dissolution and presides over Jīva-tattva and Ahaṅkāra.
meaning_deep: In Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya 1.7 and Taittirīya Bhāṣya 1.1.13 (`saṅkarṣaṇaḥ suvarnāmā`), Saṅkarṣaṇa (accompanied by Jayā-rūpā Lakṣmī) orchestrates cosmic withdrawal without any internal difference from Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.

meaning_short: Pradyumna (from `pra + dyumna` — pre-eminent radiance and wealth) is the third eternal Vyūha form of Bhagavān who initiates cosmic creation and awakens knowledge.
meaning_deep: Accompanied by Kṛti-rūpā Ramā (MBTN 1.7), Bhagavān Pradyumna brings forth sentient beings into manifest creation and illumines the intellect (`bhuvo nāmā bāhū pradyumna īritaḥ` — TTB 1.1.13).

meaning_short: Aniruddha ('He whose will and power are obstructed by none') is the fourth eternal Vyūha form of Bhagavān, presiding with Śānti-devī over cosmic preservation and protection.
meaning_deep: In MBTN 1.8–9 and Taittirīya Bhāṣya 1.1.18 (`ya eṣa hṛdayākāśas tv aniruddhas tu tadgataḥ`), Aniruddha shelters disembodied souls with their karmas, fashions their bodies from Brahmā downward, and sustains every breath.

english_glosses: Keshava; Lord of Brahma and Shiva
phonetic_aliases: keshava; kesava; keshavah; केशव

meaning_short: Keśava is He who governs and empowers both 'Ka' (Caturmukha Brahmā) and 'Īśa' (Rudra), and whose luminous rays ('keśāḥ') illumine sun, moon, and cosmos.

english_glosses: Govinda; Lord of Vedic speech and Earth

meaning_short: Govinda is He who is known through the 'Go's (sacred Vedic words) and who rescues and sustains the Earth, the Vedas, the senses, and cows.
meaning_deep: In Sanskrit 'go' signifies Vedic speech, earth, rays of light, senses, and cattle: Govinda is therefore the epistemological goal of all Vedic śabda (`sarva-vedānta-vedya`), the Varāha rescuer of Earth, and Gopāla of Vraja.

meaning_short: Madhusūdana is the Slayer of the demon Madhu who stole the Vedas, and the Destroyer of seductive, binding karmic attachments ('madhu').
meaning_deep: Fifth of the Dvādaśa-nāmas and recurrent epithet in the Bhagavadgītā, Madhusūdana removes tamasic delusion (Madhu-kaiṭabha) so that pure Vedic wisdom shines unhindered.

english_glosses: Trivikrama; Three-Striding Cosmic Lord

lakshana_iast: trīn lokān trīn vedān guṇatrayaṃ ca vikramate'tikramya vyāpnotīti trivikramaḥ |
meaning_short: Trivikrama is He who strode across the three worlds with three cosmic steps and whose glory pervades and transcends the three Vedas and three Guṇas.
meaning_deep: Celebrated in the Vedic Viṣṇu-sūkta (`idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame tredhā nidadhe padam`) and Madhvācārya's namesake Pandit Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya's *Vāyustuti*, Trivikrama's lotus-foot pierced the shell of Brahmāṇḍa, releasing the purifying Virajā-Gaṅgā.

meaning_short: Vāmana is both the enchanting Brahmācārī Avatāra and the adorable ('vāma' = lovely/choiceworthy) thumb-sized Bimba Lord seated in the centre of the heart-lotus, worshipped by all the senses and deities.

meaning_short: Hṛṣīkeśa is the Sovereign Master and Inner Director of all cognitive and motor faculties ('hṛṣīkāṇi') as well as the gladdening rays of sun and moon.
meaning_deep: In Bhagavadgītābhāṣya, Arjuna's addressing Kṛṣṇa as 'Hṛṣīkeśa' carries profound philosophical weight: He who rules every sense and mind from within alone knows how to steady the bewildered seeker's buddhi.

english_glosses: Damodara; Cord-Bound Beloved of Yashoda

meaning_short: Dāmodara is He who graciously allowed Yaśodā's cord of love ('dāma') to bind His waist, who holds all worlds ('dāmāni') in His belly ('udara'), and who is realized through spiritual discipline ('dama').
meaning_deep: Crowning the Dvādaśa-mūrtis (TSS 1.13), Dāmodara exemplifies `bhakta-parādhīnatva` without compromising `svātantrya`: the Unbound Infinite lets pure love tie Him (`dāmodaratvaṃ bhaktavaśyatvam`).

english_glosses: Acyuta; the Infallible and Imperishable One

meaning_short: Acyuta ('the Unfallen / Inexhaustible') is He who never suffers diminution or lapse from His essence, bliss, knowledge, or power — and who never lets His devotees fall.
meaning_deep: Saluted by Madhvācārya in the opening of Aitareya Bhāṣya (`nārāyaṇaṃ nikhilapūrṇaguṇaikadehaṃ sarvajñam acyutam apetasamastadoṣam`), Acyuta refutes every theory that Brahman undergoes real modification or self-forgetting in avatāras or creation.

meaning_short: Janārdana (from `jana + √ard` 'gatau yācane hiṃsāyāṃ ca') is He who crushes wicked forces, terminates rebirth ('jana'), and is entreated by wise seekers for liberation.

meaning_short: Prājña ('Supreme Omniscient One', from `prakarṣeṇa jānāti`) is the third Māṇḍūkya form of Bhagavān seated in the heart-lotus, embracing the soul in deep sleep and revered as its Bimba-rūpa.

lakshana_iast: sarvasya hi praṇetṛtvāt prāṇo nārāyaṇaḥ paraḥ | vāyukeśavayoḥ prāṇanāma sarvapraṇāyanāt ||
meaning_short: Prāṇa (from `pra + √an` / `pra + √nī` — supreme leader and animator of all) primarily denotes Supreme Nārāyaṇa (`bṛhat-prāṇaḥ keśavaḥ`) and secondarily Mukhyaprāṇa Vāyu, highest of all Jīvas.
meaning_deep: In Māṇḍūkya Bhāṣya 1.12, Aitareya Bhāṣya 2.1.15, and Brahmasūtra 1.1.23 (`ata eva prāṇaḥ`), Madhvācārya clarifies the dual Vedic usage of 'Prāṇa': where supreme independence and mokṣa-giving are taught, Prāṇa is Viṣṇu Himself; as foremost servant, mediator (`jīvanopāya`), and future Brahmā, Prāṇa is Mukhyaprāṇa Vāyu.
