english_glosses: Agni; sacred fire; Foremost Guide
phonetic_aliases: agni; agnih; vaishvanara; अग्नि
lakshana_deva: अग्निशब्दोऽयमग्र एवाभिपूज्यताम् । अग्र्यत्वमग्रनेतृत्वमत्तिमङ्गागनेतृताम् ॥ वक्ति विष्णोः ।
lakshana_iast: agniśabdo'yam agra evābhipūjyatām | agryatvam agranetṛtvam attim aṅgāganetṛtām || vakti viṣṇoḥ |
meaning_short: Commenting on the very first word of the Ṛgveda (`agnim īḷe`), Madhvācārya derives 'Agni' as naming Supreme Viṣṇu: Foremost in worship, Supreme Leader ('agra-nī'), Cosmic Devourer at pralaya ('atti'), and Mover of body and limbs ('aṅga-netṛ').
meaning_deep: In Ṛgbhāṣya 1.1.1 and Anubhāṣya 1.2 (`praṇetā jyotir ityādyaiḥ prasiddhair anyavastuṣu | ucyate viṣṇur evaikaḥ`), Madhvācārya demonstrates his golden hermeneutic of Vedic polysemy: every Vedic deity-name denotes its cosmic god by ordinary convention, AND supremely denotes Nārāyaṇa (indwelling that god) by plenitude of root-qualities!

lakshana_deva: स इन्द्रः परमैश्वर्यादशत्रुः समवर्जनात् । इदं पश्यतीति वा परमात्मेन्द्रः ॥
lakshana_iast: sa indraḥ paramaiśvaryād aśatruḥ samavarjanāt | idaṃ paśyatīti vā paramātmendraḥ ||
meaning_short: In Vedic nirukti, 'Indra' primarily denotes Paramātman Viṣṇu from His absolute supreme sovereignty ('paramaiśvaryāt' — √ind) and direct vision of reality ('idam adarśam' — Aitareya 1.3.14).
meaning_deep: In Bṛhadāraṇyaka Bhāṣya 1.6.19 and MBTN 1.100–101 (citing ṚV 6.47.16–17), Madhvācārya shows how Vedic Indra-hymns proclaim the Supreme Peerless Ruler (`aśatruḥ samavarjanāt`) who humbles the proud and uplifts the humble.

lakshana_iast: tat tu pūrṇatvataḥ pūṣā viṣṇur darśayati svayam | satyadharmāya bhaktāya sūryamaṇḍalagaṃ mukham ||
meaning_short: In Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad 15 (`pūṣann ekarṣe`), 'Pūṣan' denotes Bhagavān Viṣṇu by virtue of His plenary fullness ('pūrṇatvataḥ') and universal nourishment (`√puṣ`), dwelling within the golden solar orb.
meaning_deep: Commenting on `hiraṇmayena pātreṇa satyasyāpihitaṃ mukham`, Madhvācārya reveals that the dazzling solar disk veils the blissful lotus-face of Satya-Nārāyaṇa, which Lord Pūṣan Himself unveils unto His true devotee.

lakshana_deva: उच्छब्दवाच्याः प्राणाद्या वागाद्या गीरितीरिताः । अन्नाद्या थमिति प्रोक्तास्तेषूद्गीथो हरिः स्थितः ॥
lakshana_iast: ucchabdavācyāḥ prāṇādyā vāgādyā gīr itīritāḥ | annādyā tham iti proktās teṣūdgītho hariḥ sthitaḥ ||
meaning_short: In Chāndogya Upaniṣad, 'Udgītha' signifies Bhagavān Hari who abides indwelling within 'Ut' (Prāṇa and skies), 'Gīḥ' (Vedic speech), and 'Tham' (sustaining food/earth), and who is chanted aloft as Oṃ.
meaning_deep: A jewel of syllable-by-syllable Vedic nirukti (`ut + gīḥ + tham`) in Chāndogya Bhāṣya 1.1.28: rather than treating Udgītha as mere ritual Sāma-chant, Madhvācārya unveils Hari Himself as the living Udgītha celebrated by every Sāma-singer.

lakshana_iast: ṛṅnāmā jñānarūpatvāt | ṛg arcanāyāḥ svīkārād bhagavān hariḥ ||
meaning_short: 'Ṛk' primarily names Bhagavān Hari Himself because His essence is pure Omniscient Knowledge ('jñānarūpatvāt') and because He graciously accepts all worship and praise ('arcanā').
meaning_deep: In Chāndogya Bhāṣya 1.7.5 and Taittirīya Bhāṣya 1.2.9, Madhvācārya shows that Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman are not only the three Vedic corpora (`aparā vidyā` when read merely philologically, `parā vidyā` when read as revealing Viṣṇu — MUN 1.3), but direct names of Bhagavān!

lakshana_iast: yaḥ paśyati svayaṃ vākyaṃ sa ṛṣis tasya kīrtitaḥ | ṛṣiś ca devataiko'haṃ tārādīnāṃ viśeṣataḥ ||
meaning_short: A Ṛṣi is a Seer — not an author — who directly perceives ('paśyati') the eternal, uncreated Vedic mantra by yogic intuition (`ṛṣir darśanāt`); supremely, Bhagavān Viṣṇu Himself is the Primeval Ṛṣi of all Vedas.
meaning_deep: In Ṛgbhāṣya 1.1.9, Taittirīya Bhāṣya 1.1.21 (`ity uvāca svayaṃ viṣṇur vedadraṣṭā guṇādhikaḥ`), and Tantrasārasaṅgraha 1.17, Madhvācārya anchors `Veda-apauruṣeyatva`: Viāsa, Viśvāmitra, and Vasiṣṭha are mantra-draṣṭās (seers of pre-existing eternal mantras), never mantra-kartās.

meaning_deep: In Aitareya Bhāṣya 2.1.15, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Bhāṣya 1.3.20, and Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.22 (`strīśabdāś ca niṣedhārthāḥ sarve'pi brahmavācakāḥ`), Madhvācārya shows that even feminine Vedic nouns like Bṛhatī, Śrī, and Gāyatrī ultimately celebrate the boundless plenitude of Bhagavān alongside Ramā and Sarasvatī.

meaning_short: The four sacred Vedic Vyāhṛtis — Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahaḥ — signify Bhagavān's four Vyūha forms (Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva) and His fullness, sovereignty, and infinite bliss.

meaning_short: The visarga 'aḥ' signifies Bhagavān Ardhagarbha — He who holds the entire cosmos effortlessly within a tiny fraction of His infinite being — and in Aitareya Śruti directly names Brahman ('Aḥ iti Brahma'). Crowns the 16 Svaras with Aitareya Śruti's 'Aḥ iti Brahma' and TSS 1.7's 'Ardhagarbha', harmonized with Tāratamya-governed Rudra/Sūrya and Pāṇinian visarga.
meaning_deep: [Varṇa #16 · Svara · Praṇava-Ukāra (Taijasa-pāda)] Closing the sixteen Svaras, 'aḥ' carries dual majesty in Madhvācārya's works: in Tantrasārasaṅgraha 1.7 He is Ardhagarbha (cradling all brahmāṇḍas in a fraction of His form, `ekāṃśena sthito jagat` — BG 10.42), and in Aitareya Bhāṣya 2.3.32 'Aḥ' is the primeval Vedic name of Parabrahman.

lakshana_deva: कं सुखं ज्ञानं च पिलति ददाति पाति वेति ककारवाच्यः कपिलः ।
lakshana_iast: kaṃ sukhaṃ jñānaṃ ca pilati dadāti pāti veti kakāravācyaḥ kapilaḥ |
meaning_short: The first consonant 'ka' signifies Bhagavān Kapila — the giver of supreme bliss ('ka') and luminous wisdom, primal teacher of Sāṅkhya-tattvajñāna. Classic flagship ekākṣara: Bhagavān Kapila & 'Kaṃ Brahma' in Sarvamūla, plus Amarakośa 3.3.1's Vāyu, Brahmā, Sūrya, Ātman (m.) and head, water, bliss (n.), alongside interrogative 'kim' and taddhita '-ka'.
meaning_deep: [Varṇa #17 · Ka-varga · Praṇava-Makāra (Prājña-pāda)] Across Vedic koshas 'ka' denotes bliss (`kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma` — Chāndogya 4.10.5). Madhvācārya identifies 'ka' with Bhagavān Kapila, the canonical Jñānāvatāra who revealed authentic twenty-four-tattva ontology and bhakti-yoga to Devahūti and Brahmā.

meaning_short: The fifty-first crowning syllable 'kṣa' (Meru-varṇa, uniting 'ka' + 'ṣa') signifies Bhagavān Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha (Akṣa) — the Imperishable Destroyer of all sin, fear, and ignorance. Crowning 51st Meru-syllable ('ka' Kapila + 'ṣa' Ṣaḍguṇa): Bhagavān Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha (Akṣa) in Mādhva Mātṛkā-nyāsa AND Puruṣottamadeva's Ekākṣarakośa ('kṣo nṛsiṃhe ca kṣetre ca')!
meaning_deep: [Varṇa #51 · Meru-Varṇa · Ekapañcāśad-Mātṛkā Culmination] Completing the fifty-one-syllable (`ekapañcāśad-varṇa`) Mātṛkā mala from 'a' (Aja) to 'kṣa' (`akṣamālā`), 'kṣa' fuses 'ka' (Kapila — supreme bliss) and 'ṣa' (Ṣaḍguṇa — plenary sixfold majesty) into the blazing Ekākṣara bīja of Bhagavān Nṛsiṃha, who annihilates (`kṣapayati`) all bondage.

meaning_deep: Among all monosyllabic words in Sanskrit lexicography, 'go' (`gauḥ`) stands pre-eminent in Amarasiṃha's Nānārthavarga (3.3.25). Śrī Madhvācārya shows across Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, Bhagavadgītābhāṣya, and Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya that every one of Amarakośa's nine senses converges on Viṣṇu as Govinda and Gopati: known through Vedic speech (`vāk`), Lord of Vaikuṇṭha/Svarga, Uplifter of Earth (`bhū`) as Varāha, Inner Director of eyes/senses (`netra/hṛṣīka`), and Effulgence within solar rays (`ghṛṇi`).

meaning_short: Both the primal Vedic Vyāhṛti ('Bhūḥ' = Plenary Bhagavān Viṣṇu) and the classic Amarakośa monosyllable denoting Earth, Bhūdevī, locus/ground, sacrificial site, and pure Being.
meaning_deep: Formed with root-zero suffix `kvip` from `√bhū sattāyām`, 'bhūḥ' functions simultaneously as an indeclinable Vedic Vyāhṛti (Amarakośa 3.4) and as a feminine root-noun (Amarakośa 2.1.2 `भूर्भूमिः अचला अनन्ता`). In Mādhva Vedānta, its highest sense is Bhagavān Viṣṇu (Aniruddha/Viśva) whose plenary existence grounds every locus (`ādhāra`).

english_glosses: Mahālakṣmī (Mā — Consort of Mādhava); Supreme Measurer & Knower (Hari); valid knowledge / measure (pramā); mother (mātā); beauty / lustre (śobhā); do not! — prohibitive particle (niṣedha)
phonetic_aliases: ma; maa; ma-lakshmi; madhava-ma; मा
lakshana_deva: इन्दिरा लोकमाता मा क्षीरोदतनया रमा । मा निषेधे च माने च ॥
lakshana_iast: indirā lokamātā mā kṣīrodatanayā ramā | mā niṣedhe ca māne ca ||
meaning_short: Famous Amarakośa monosyllable naming Goddess Mahālakṣmī ('Mā', AK 1.1.28), liberating knowledge/measurement ('māna'), mother, and the prohibitive particle 'do not' (AK 3.4).
meaning_deep: In Amarakośa 1.1.28, 'Mā' stands right at the head of Mahālakṣmī's names (`indirā lokamātā mā`), whence Viṣṇu is `Mā-dhava` (Consort of Mā) and `Mā-pati`. Simultaneously in Amarakośa 3.4 (`Avyayavarga`) and Pāṇini 3.3.175 (`माङि लुङ्`), `mā` is the canonical prohibitive particle (`mā śucaḥ` — 'grieve not!', BG 18.66).

meaning_short: Revered monosyllable of Amarakośa and Vedic Śrī-Sūkta denoting Mahālakṣmī, the Vedic Triad, royal majesty, intellect, beauty, auspicious wealth, and sacred grace.
meaning_deep: Derived from `√śriञ् sevāyām` ('to serve / resort to'), 'śrīḥ' is explained across Amarakośa (1.1.28 & 3.3 Nānārthavarga) and Medinīkośa as encompassing divine Ramā, the three Vedas, dharma-artha-kāma prosperity, beauty, and wisdom. In Mādhva theology, every auspicious splendour in creation is presided over by Mahālakṣmī, who eternally resorts solely to Śrīपति Nārāyaṇa.

lakshana_iast: buddhir manīṣā dhiṣaṇā dhīḥ prajñā śemuṣī matiḥ | dhyāyate'nayā dhatte tattvam iti dhīḥ ||
meaning_short: Canonical monosyllable of Amarakośa 1.5.1 and the Gāyatrī Mantra — signifying luminous intellect ('prajñā'), loving meditation, Vedic knowledge, and sacred action.
meaning_deep: Derived from `√dhyai cintāyām` (or `√dhā dhāraṇe`), 'dhīḥ' is placed at the heart of Amarakośa's Dhīvarga (`buddhir manīṣā dhiṣaṇā dhīḥ prajñā`) and Yāska's Nighaṇṭu (where `dhīḥ` denotes both `prajñā` and `karma`). In Śrī Madhvācārya's Gāyatrī-vyākhyāna and Ṛgbhāṣya, Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa is both the Inner Impeller (`pracodayitā`) of every soul's `dhī` and Plenary Consciousness itself.

meaning_deep: From `√gṝ śabde` ('to proclaim, invoke, praise'), 'gīḥ' (`giraḥ` pl.) is Amarasiṃha's canonical synonym for articulate speech and Goddess Sarasvatī (`gīr vāg vāṇī sarasvatī`, AK 1.6.1; `gīṣpati` = Bṛhaspati/Brahmā). In Mādhva Vedānta (`akṣarāṇām akāro'smi... girām asmy ekam akṣaram` — BG 10.25), the highest `gīḥ` is Praṇava and the unauthored Veda praising Nārāyaṇa.

meaning_short: Foundational consonant-stem monosyllable (`vāc` → `vāk`, AK 1.6.1) signifying the unauthored Veda, Mahālakṣmī/Sarasvatī, articulate speech, and authoritative testimony.
meaning_deep: From `√vac paribhāṣaṇe`, `vāk` spans earthly utterance (`vaikharī`) up to the eternal, uncreated Vedic revelation (`nityā vāk` — ṚV 10.125 Vāgāmbhṛṇī Sūkta). In Śrī Madhvācārya's Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya and Ṛgbhāṣya, `Vāk` is supremely Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī proclaiming the glory of Supreme Brahman (`yaṃ kāmaye taṃ tam ugraṃ kṛṇomi`).

lakshana_deva: द्यौर्दिवोऽभ्रं व्योम पुष्करम् । द्यौः स्वर्गगगनद्युतिवासरेशु ॥
lakshana_iast: dyaur divo'bhraṃ vyoma puṣkaram | dyauḥ svargagaganadyutivāsareṣu ||
meaning_short: Classic diphthongal nominative (`dyauḥ` from stem `div`, AK 1.2.1 & 3.3) denoting Heaven, Sky, Day, Radiance, and the luminous spiritual abode of Viṣṇu.
meaning_deep: From `√divu krīḍā-vijigīṣā-vyavahāra-dyuti-stuti-moda-mada-svapna-kānti-gatiṣu` (Dhātupāṭha 4.1), the monosyllable `dyauḥ` (`div`) unites sky, celestial paradise, daylight, and divine play/radiance. In Brahmasūtra 1.3.1 (`dyubhvādyāyatanaṃ svaśabdāt`), Madhvācārya shows that `dyauḥ` rests in Paramātman and in highest Vedic usage (`divo viṣṇuḥ`, `parame vyoman`) denotes Vaikuṇṭha and luminous Hari.

english_glosses: Svaḥ — Third Vyāhṛti (Self-Blissful Hari); mokṣa / Vaikuṇṭha (transcendental bliss); heaven / celestial world (svarga-loka); solar light & splendour (āditya-tejas); auspicious welfare (sukha / maṅgala)
phonetic_aliases: svah; svar; suvah; svarga-svah; स्वः; स्वर्
lakshana_deva: स्वर्गव्ययम् स्वर्गनाकत्रिदिवत्रिदशालयाः । सुष्ठु रमयतीति स्वः परमात्मा ॥
lakshana_iast: svar avyayam svarganākatridivatridāśālayāḥ | suṣṭhu ramayatīti svaḥ paramātmā ||
meaning_short: Indeclinable Amarakośa monosyllable (`svar` → `svaḥ`, AK 1.1.6 & 3.4) and third Gāyatrī Vyāhṛti — signifying Self-Blissful Bhagavān, Mokṣa/Vaikuṇṭha, Svarga, and solar radiance.
meaning_deep: Listed first among all names of heaven in Amarakośa 1.1.6 (`svar avyayaṃ svarga-nāka-tridiva...`) and reiterated in Avyayavarga (3.4), `svaḥ` is also the third sacred Vedic Vyāhṛti (`bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ`). In Taittirīya Bhāṣya 1.5 and Tantrasārasaṅgraha, Śrī Madhvācārya derives `svaḥ` as naming Bhagavān Viṣṇu (Saṅkarṣaṇa/Prājña) who delights independently in His own essence (`sva-ramaṇa`) and bestows supreme bliss.

english_glosses: spatial direction / cardinal quarter (kāṣṭhā); eternal unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa); scriptural injunction / pointing out (upadeśa); presiding Dig-devatās & auditory sense; Supreme Guide Hari (ādeṣṭā)

lakshana_deva: दिशस्तु ककुभः काष्ठा आशाश्च हरितश्च ताः । दिशत्यादिशति धर्ममिति दिक् ॥
lakshana_iast: diśas tu kakubhaḥ kāṣṭhā āśāś ca haritaś ca tāḥ | diśaty ādiśati dharmam iti dik ||
meaning_short: Consonant-stem Amarakośa monosyllable (`diś` → `dik`, AK 1.3.1) denoting spatial quarter, eternal Avyākṛtākāśa, scriptural directive, and the presiding deities of space and hearing.
meaning_deep: From `√diś अतिसर्जने` ('to point out, assign, instruct'), `dik` signifies the ten spatial directions (East, South-East, South, etc.) in Amarakośa 1.3.1. In Mādhva ontology (Padārthasaṅgraha & Anuvyākhyāna), pure spatial dimensionality (`dik` / `avyākṛtākāśa`) is eternal (`nitya`), real, and distinct from elemental `bhūtākāśa`, while Dig-devatās preside over both the quarters and the auditory faculty (`śrotra`).

lakshana_deva: आपः स्त्री भूम्नि वार्वारि सलिलं कमलं जलम् । आप्नोति रक्षति चाप्याययतीत्यापः ॥
lakshana_iast: āpaḥ strī bhūmni vār vāri salilaṃ kamalaṃ jalam | āpnoti rakṣati cāpyāyayatīty āpaḥ ||
meaning_short: Pluralia tantum monosyllabic stem (`ap` → nom. pl. `āpaḥ`, AK 1.10.3) signifying water, the primordial Nāra-waters indwelt by Nārāyaṇa, Varuṇa, and All-Pervading Viṣṇu.
meaning_deep: Amarakośa 1.10.3 notes the strict grammatical signature of `ap`: feminine and obligatorily plural (`āpaḥ strī bhūmni`, acc. `apaḥ`, instr. `adbhiḥ`). Derived from `√āpḷ vyāptau` ('to pervade/obtain'), in Aitareya Bhāṣya and Āpohिṣṭhā Sūkta commentary Śrī Madhvācārya reveals that `Āpaḥ` in supreme Vedic usage denotes Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa who pervades (`āpnoti`) and nourishes all worlds.

english_glosses: self-luminous Consciousness of Brahman; light / radiance / lustre (kānti / dīpti); solar ray (kiraṇa); reflection / likeness (pratibimba / chāyā); star / asterism (nakṣatra — bham)
phonetic_aliases: bhah; bha-lustre; bhaa; kanti-bha; भाः; भा
lakshana_deva: भाः कान्तौ रश्मिच्छायासु भं नक्षत्रे ग्रहेऽपि च । तस्य भासा सर्वमिदं विभाति ॥
lakshana_iast: bhāḥ kāntau raśmicchāyāsu bhaṃ nakṣatre grahe'pi ca | tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti ||
meaning_short: Luminous Amarakośa monosyllable (`bhāḥ` f. / `bham` n., AK 1.3 & 3.3) denoting spiritual and physical radiance, sunbeam, beauty, reflection, and star/planet.
meaning_deep: From `√bhā dīptau` (Dhātupāṭha 2.42), feminine `bhāḥ` signifies light, beauty, ray, and reflection, while neuter `bham` denotes asterism/nakṣatra and zodiacal sign (Amarakośa 1.3.21 `भं नक्षत्रम्`). In Kaṭha/Muṇḍaka Bhāṣya (`tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti`) and `Bhārata`-nirukti (`bhā-rata`), Śrī Madhvācārya shows that all cosmic illumination depends on Bhagavān's self-luminous `bhā` (jñāna-prabhā).

english_glosses: imperishable spiritual treasure (jñāna-bhakti-sampat); wealth / riches / property (dhana); gold & jewels (hiraṇya); liberating grace bestowed by Hari; offering / gift (dāna)
phonetic_aliases: rah; rai; raye; ra-wealth; राः; रै
lakshana_deva: द्रविणं तरमृक्थं श्रीः राः स्युरर्थसम्पदि । अग्ने नय सुपथा राये ॥
lakshana_iast: draviṇaṃ taram ṛkthaṃ śrīḥ rāḥ syur arthasampadi | agne naya supathā rāye ||
meaning_short: Classical diphthongal Amarakośa monosyllable (`rai` → nom. sg. `rāḥ`, dat. `rāye`, AK 2.9.90) denoting spiritual and worldly wealth, gold, and the treasure of mokṣa.
meaning_deep: celebrated in the closing Vedic prayer of Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad 18 (`agne naya supathā rāye asmān` — 'O Agni-nāmaka Hari, lead us by the auspicious non-returning path to supreme spiritual wealth!'), `rāḥ` (`rai`) is explained by Śrī Madhvācārya in Īśāvāsya Bhāṣya as denoting foremost the imperishable wealth of Mokṣa (`mukti-sampat`) and Aparokṣajñāna, while Amarakośa 2.9.90 records its worldly sense of riches and gold.

meaning_short: Consonant-stem Amarakośa monosyllable (`dhur` → nom. sg. `dhūḥ`, AK 2.8.55 & 3.3) denoting chariot-yoke, burden of responsibility, forefront/summit, and the cosmic governance borne effortlessly by Hari.

lakshana_deva: पूः स्त्री पुरी नगरी वा शरीरब्रह्माण्डदुर्गेषु च । पुरि शयनात् पुरुषो हरिः ॥
lakshana_iast: pūḥ strī purī nagarī vā śarīrabrahmāṇḍadurgeṣu ca | puri śayanāt puruṣo hariḥ ||
meaning_short: Consonant-stem Amarakośa monosyllable (`pur` → nom. sg. `pūḥ`, AK 2.2.1 & 3.3) signifying city, citadel, fullness, and the living body (`pura`) indwelt by Bhagavān Puruṣa.
meaning_deep: From `√pṝ pālane pūraṇe ca` ('to protect and fill'), `pūḥ` (`pur`) is Amarasiṃha's opening word of Puravarga (`pūḥ strī purī nagaryau vā`, AK 2.2.1) and in Nānārthavarga denotes both town/fortress and the physical/subtle body (`deha`). Across Upaniṣad Bhāṣyas (`puraś चक्रे द्विपदः` — BṛU 2.5.18) and Bhagavadgītā 5.13, `pūḥ` is the sacred body-citadel governed from within by the Bimba-form of Viṣṇu (`Puruṣa`).

lakshana_iast: bhūtadhātrī ratnagarbhā jagatī sāgarāmbarā kṣmā kṣoṇī jyāvaniḥ | sarvaṃ kṣamata iti kṣmā ||
meaning_short: striking three-consonant-onset Amarakośa monosyllable (`kṣmā`, AK 2.1.2–3) denoting all-forbearing Earth, Goddess Bhūdevī, royal realm (`kṣmāpati`), and the numeral 1 in Jyotiṣa.
meaning_deep: Compressed from `√kṣamūष् sahane` ('to endure patiently'), `kṣmā` is one of Sanskrit's boldest single-syllable nominals (`k + ṣ + m + ā`), celebrated in Amarakośa's Bhūmivarga (2.1.2–3) and classical kāvya (`kṣmābhṛt` = mountain or king). In Mādhva theology, Bhūdevī (`Kṣmā`) is the eternal Śakti-aspect of Ramā upheld by Lord Bhū-Varāha (`Kṣmāpati`).

english_glosses: Sat — Defectless Supreme Brahman (Viṣṇu); real / existent / unsublated (vidyamāna); good / virtuous / saintly sage (sādhu); auspicious / praiseworthy / noble (praśasta); steadfastness in devotion & yajña (BG 17.26–27); Vedic truth & eternal Prakṛti/Kāla
phonetic_aliases: sat; sad; sat-brahman; sadbhava; सत्
lakshana_deva: सत् सत्ये साधुविद्यमानप्रशस्तेषु । सद्भावे साधुभावे च सदित्येतत् प्रयुज्यते ॥
lakshana_iast: sat satye sādhuvidyamānapraśasteṣu | sadbhāve sādhubhāve ca sad ity etat prayujyate ||
meaning_short: Canonical monosyllable of Amarakośa 3.3 and Bhagavadgītā 17.26–27 — signifying Defectless Supreme Brahman, objective reality (`sadbhāva`), moral goodness (`sādhubhāva`), noble sages (`santaḥ`), and auspicious deeds.
meaning_deep: Formed as the present participle (`√as bhuvi + śatṛ` → `sat`) and expounded explicitly by Lord Kṛṣṇa in Bhagavadgītā 17.26–27 (`sadbhāve sādhubhāve ca...`) as well as Amarakośa's Nānārthavarga (`satya-sādhu-vidyamāna-praśasteṣu`), `sat` refutes illusionism in Mādhva Vedānta: Viṣṇu is `Svatantra-Sat` (Independent, Defectless Plenitude) while souls and cosmos are `Asvatantra-Sat` (genuinely existent dependents).

english_glosses: Cit — Self-Luminous Omniscient Brahman; pure consciousness / sentient awareness (caitanya); sentient soul (cetana-jīva); indefinite particle (-cit: kaścit, kadācit); sacred piling of Vedic fire-altar (agni-citi)
phonetic_aliases: cit; chit; chaitanya; saccidananda; चित्
lakshana_deva: चित् संज्ञाने चैतन्ये च निपातोऽनियमेऽपि च । चिदानन्दमयो हरिः ॥
lakshana_iast: cit saṃjñāne caitanye ca nipāto'niyame'pi ca | cidānandamayo hariḥ ||
meaning_short: Essential monosyllable of Vedānta and Amarakośa — denoting self-luminous Consciousness (`caitanya`), sentient beings (`cetana`), and the enclitic indefinite particle `-cit` (`kaścit`, `kiñcit`).
meaning_deep: Derived from `√citी संज्ञाने` ('to cognize, be conscious', Dhātupāṭha 1.38 + `kvip`), `cit` stands as the middle jewel of `Sat-Cit-Ānanda`. In Mādhva Siddhānta, Viṣṇu is `Svatantra-Cit` (Infinite, Untainted Self-Luminous Omniscience), Lakṣmī is `Nitya-muktā Cit`, and Jīvas are atomic `Pratibimba-Cit` distinct from insentient `jaḍa` matter (`acetana`).

lakshana_deva: खमिन्द्रिये पुरे क्षेत्रे शून्ये बिन्दौ विहायसि । संवेदने देवलोके शर्मण्यपि नपुंसकम् ॥ कं ब्रह्म खं ब्रह्म ॥
lakshana_iast: kham indriye pure kṣetre śūnye bindau vihāyasi | saṃvedane devaloke śarmaṇy api napuṃsakam || kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma ||
meaning_short: Classic neuter Amarakośa & Chāndogya monosyllable (`kham`) — uniting space/sky, sense-organ, heaven, zero/dot, cognition, happiness, and All-Pervasive Blissful Brahman (`kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma`, ChU 4.10.5).
meaning_deep: In Amarakośa 1.2.1 (`vyoma puṣkaram ambaraṃ nabhaḥ kham`) and the Nānārtha kośas, `kham` spans nine concrete and philosophical domains: sky, sense-organ (whence `su-kha` = agreeable to spiritual/inner sense, `duḥ-kha`, `hṛṣīka`), zero (`ख-हर`), heaven, cavity, and consciousness. In Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5 (`kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma`), Śrī Madhvācārya explains that `Kham` names Supreme Brahman because He is infinitely pervasive like space and replete with unalloyed bliss!
